parole.significato: Used to form the feminine forms of most nouns and adjectives.
parole.testo: From Arabic ـَة (-a), reinforced by Sicilian and Italian -a, which are unrelated but used similarly.

parole.significato: Used to form the pronominal forms of the cardinal numbers from 11 to 19; -teen.
parole.testo: From common dialectal Arabic -aʿš, -āš, from عَشَرة (ʕašara, “ten”), whence Maltese għaxra. There is evidence that the underlying għ had already been vocalised in this ending before the same happened as a general development in Maltese (hence also the lack of it in the spelling). We find the same vo

parole.significato: a plural suffix used in a few nouns that come in pairs
parole.testo: From Arabic ـَيْنِ (-ayni), oblique case form of ـَانِ (-āni), the dual suffix.

parole.significato: a derivational suffix, chiefly creating adjectives from nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic ـِيّ (-iyy), from Proto-Semitic, from Proto-Afroasiatic.
Inherited from Arabic ـِي (-ī, “possessive suffix, 1st person singular”).

parole.significato: a plural suffix used in some nouns, chiefly ones of Arabic origin and/or ending in -a
parole.testo: From Arabic ـَات (-āt), feminine and non-personal plural ending.

parole.significato: a common plural suffix for nouns
parole.testo: From Arabic ـِيَّات (-iyyāt), feminine plural of the derivational suffix ـِيّ (-iyy), whence Maltese -i. Natively used with nouns in -ija, then probably first extended to Sicilian borrowings in -i and finally also to consonant-final borrowings.

parole.significato: Used to form the attributive form of cardinal numbers 11 to 19.
parole.testo: From the syllable -ar in Arabic عَشَر (ʕašar, “ten”). The same alternation between absolute and attributive form is found in most modern dialects of Arabic, though generally with the original consonant r preserved. Cognate with Tunisian Arabic ن (n). Compare North Levantine Arabic تنعش (tnaʕš, “twel
From Arabic ـِينَ (-īna), oblique case form of ـُونَ (-ūna), masculine personal plural suffix.
From Arabic ـكَ m (-ka), ـكِ f (-ki).

parole.significato: 1st-person singular pronominal suffix, attached to verbs: me
3rd-person masculine singular pronominal suffix: his, him
Used together with the particle ma to negate verbs and adverbs
parole.testo: From Arabic شَيْء (šayʔ, “thing”). The same negation suffix is found in most North African and some Levantine dialects of Arabic.

Possibly from Arabic أيّل (ʔayyil, ʔuyyal, “wild goat, ibex” as well as “deer”). The already ambiguous word may have been transferred to the porcupine, perhaps on account of its spines vis-à-vis the wild goat’s pointed horns. It must be considered that many of the inherited Arabic animal names lost
From Arabic أَكْثَر شَيْء (ʔakṯar šayʔ, “mostly, for the most part; most, to the greatest degree”). Analysable as aktar + -x.
From the proper noun Alla (“God”), from Arabic الله (allāh). The Arabic is not used as a common noun, for which related إلٰه (ʔilāh).

parole.significato: to command; to order; to decree
parole.testo: From Arabic أَمَرَ (ʔamara). An obsolete word that was revived by purists in the early 20th century on the basis of early Maltese sources.

From Arabic رَطْب (raṭb). The Maltese feminine and plural go back directly to the Arabic adjective, while the masculine is the original comparative reinterpreted as the basic form by analogy with other adjectives for physical qualities and defects (compare aħrax, oħxon, etc.).

parole.significato: a piece of news; a notice, message, report
parole.testo: From Arabic أَخْبار (ʔaḵbār), plural of خَبَر (ḵabar). The feminine gender in Maltese is a remnant of the original plural construction.
Inherited from Arabic نَحْنُ (naḥnu). Compare Egyptian Arabic احنا (eḥna).
From Arabic أَحْرَش (ʔaḥraš, “rough, coarse”). Unrelated to English harsh, though speakers may now identify them with each other (cf. especially the feminine form).
From dialectal Arabic. Compare Hijazi Arabic أح (aḥḥ), and Hebrew אח (ákh).
From Arabic آخِر (ʔāḵir) with irregular gemination, perhaps after ewwel (“first”).

parole.significato: with (chiefly an ingredient, means, concomitant, quality)

parole.testo: From Arabic بَغَضَ (baḡaḍa, “to hate”). Unrelated with the family of bgħid (“far”), from Arabic بَعِيد (baʕīd).

parole.significato: a person who has the habit of touching things or people when talking
harrier, especially the western marsh harrier
parole.testo: Alteration of older bagħdam, probably from *bugħ(a)dam, from bu + għadam, literally “the one with the bones”, probably referring to its pellet. Għadam is here an obsolete plural from Arabic عِظام (ʕiẓām), which explains the final stress.

parole.significato: to whitewash, to paint a wall

parole.testo: From Arabic بِأُنْسٍ (biʔunsin, literally “with companionship”). Hence doublet of nies.

From Arabic بَقِيَ (baqiya). The final root letter għ was added by analogy: When għ began to be vowelised, the paradigm generally remained distinct from the paradigm of actual vocalic verbs on the basis of vowel colour; compare smajt (“I heard”) from sama’, Arabic سَمِعَ (samiʕa), versus bdejt (“I b

parole.significato: to bubble up, to boil violently
parole.testo: From Arabic بَقْبَقَ (baqbaqa). Ultimately probably Onomatopoeic. Possibly doublet of bekbek (“to guzzle”).

parole.significato: bugs, bedbugs (several or the species as such)
parole.testo: From Arabic بَقّ (baqq). The similarity with the English word is coincidental.
From Arabic بِرْمِيل (birmīl, “barrel”), from Old Spanish barril, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: to wear a hood, a cowl

parole.testo: From Arabic بَرًّا (barran, “outside”). Compare Egyptian Arabic برا (barra) and the same in many or most dialects.
From Arabic بَرَّانِيّ (barrāniyy, “outer, external”). By surface analysis, barra + -ani.

parole.significato: onion (as a mass or species); several onions

parole.testo: Inherited from dialectal Arabic; compare Tunisian Arabic بص (baṣṣ, “to fart”).

parole.significato: to give birth, to breed (of animals)
to dock (to cut off a section of an animal's tail)

parole.testo: From Arabic بَطَّأَ (baṭṭaʔa, “to make or become slow”).

parole.significato: to announce, to bring news (usually of good news)

parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Arabic بهلول (“joker, fool”), which is also said to derive balalu, of similar meaning.
Inherited from Arabic بَحْرِيّ (baḥriyy). By surface analysis, baħar + -i.

parole.significato: void, emptiness, a state of being deserted
parole.testo: Inherited from dialectal Arabic. Compare Tunisian Arabic, Moroccan Arabic, and North Levantine Arabic بح (baḥḥ, “gone”, interjection).
From Arabic بَزْو (bazw), verbal noun of بَزَا (bazā), which refers to a deforming protrusion of a body part (chest, belly, back, or posterior).

From Maghrebi Arabic, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *babosu. Attested marginally in Tunisian Berber abebbuc, but there is no reason to suppose that Berber played a role in its transmission. Compare Moroccan Arabic ببوش (babbūš) and Sicilian babbaluci.
Backformation from the plural bhiem, from Arabic إِبْهَام (ʔibhām).
From Arabic بَلْغَم (balḡam), from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma).

parole.significato: to dip (immerse something shortly or partly into a liquid)
to make or cause to swallow

parole.testo: Factitive second stem derived from iblah (“stupid”), from Arabic أَبْلَه (ʔablah).
Inherited from Arabic بَنَّة (banna). Compare Moroccan Arabic بنة (banna) and Libyan Arabic بنة (banna).
Inherited from Arabic بَنَّنَ (bannana). Compare Moroccan Arabic بنن (bannan), Tunisian Arabic بنن (bannan).
Probably a metathesis of Arabic بَذْرَقَ (baḏraqa, “to waste”), itself perhaps an extended form of بَذَّرَ (baḏḏara).
From Arabic بَرَّحَ (barraḥa), second stem of بَرِحَ (bariḥa, “to depart; to take or blow away; to become manifest”). Compare Moroccan Arabic برح (barraḥ, “to make known”).

From Arabic بِطِّيخ (biṭṭīḵ). The etymologically more justified (and prescriptively preferred) spelling bettiħ is very rare in practice since the word is treated as belonging to the common measure C-e-CC-ie-C. (The phonemes /iː/ and /ɪː/ are merged before /ħ/ and /ʔ/.)
From Arabic فَزَعَ (fazaʕa) with b- from a development [fz] > [vz] > [bz] in some of the inflected forms (as also in qabeż). Compare Moroccan Arabic فزع (fzaʕ).
From Arabic بَزُّولَة (bazzūla). Compare Moroccan Arabic بزولة (bazzūla, “breast”), Tunisian Arabic بزّولة (bazzūla/bizzūla, “breast”).
From Arabic بَعِيد (baʕīd). Unrelated with the family of bagħad (“to hate”), from Arabic بَغَضَ (baḡaḍa).

parole.significato: a beast; an animal, usually either as livestock or as a wild and/or dangerous creature

parole.testo: Singulative derivation from Arabic بَدْل (badl, “changing, exchange”).
From Arabic بَاضَ (bāḍa). The phonetically expected form is archaic bad, but the vowel was altered by analogy (as in many other hollow roots).
Probably from Arabic باقِي (bāqī), باقِية (bāqiya, “rest, remainder”). Compare بَواقِي (bawāqī) in the sense of “leftovers”. Used in the same sense as Maltese in the dialect of Sfax (Tunisia).

parole.significato: tepid; cool (lacking warmth, but not really cold either; of neutral temperature)
to spend the night, to stay overnight
so that; in order that; often rather expressed in English with to + infinitive
parole.testo: Inherited from dialectal North African Arabic. By surface analysis, b’ + *iex. Cognate with Moroccan Arabic and Tunisian Arabic باش (bāš, “so that”).
From Arabic بازِل (bāzil, “fully mature, in one's prime”, of a camel or man, also “difficult, distressing”, of a problem).
Inherited from Arabic. Compare Tunisian Arabic بكري (bikri/bokri), Moroccan Arabic بكري (bakri).
Inherited from Arabic بِٱلْمَقْلُوبِ (bi-l-maqlūbi). By surface analysis, b’ + il- + maqlub.
From dialectal Arabic *بِٱللِّي (*bi-l-lī, “by that”). By surface analysis, b’ + illi. Compare Moroccan Arabic بلي (billi).

From Arabic بِناء (bināʔ). The final -i either by influence of binja or as a relict of word-final imala, for whose existence in older Maltese there is good evidence (it may have been lost through influence of the Romance feminine -a); compare also biki from Arabic بُكاء (bukāʔ).

parole.significato: to lie down (of camels), to kneel

parole.testo: From dialectal Arabic بَسّ (bass, “only”, as an interjection also “enough!”), in all likelihood from Persian بس (bas, “enough”), from Middle Persian ws (/⁠was⁠/).

parole.significato: yard, courtyard (open area by a house)
parole.testo: From Arabic بَطْحَاء (baṭḥāʔ). As usually in Maltese, the emphatic -ṭ- was made plain early on by dissimilation against the -ḥ- (otherwise we would expect *batħa). Compare Tunisian Arabic بَطْحَة.

parole.significato: appearance (the way someone or something looks, appears)
parole.testo: From Arabic بَشَرَة (bašara, “skin, especially its surface”).
From underlying Arabic بِالزَّائِدِ (bi-z-zāʔidi), from زَائِد (zāʔid, “extra, surplus”), thus originally “more than enough”.
From Arabic. Compare Arabic اِبْتَزَّ (ibtazza, “to plunder”).
From Arabic بِلَا (bi-lā, literally “with not”). By surface analysis, b’ + le.

parole.significato: rock (material, a mass or surface of it)
parole.testo: From Arabic بَلَاط (balāṭ, “tiles, paved surface”), eventually from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa).

parole.significato: human, human being, man (male or unspecified sex)
parole.testo: From Arabic اِبْن آدَم (ibn ʔādam, “man, human”, literally “son of Adam”). By surface analysis, iben + Adam. The Maltese inflections by analogy with an active participle such as riekeb, riekba, rekbin (“riding, astride”).
Inherited from Arabic بَنِين (banīn). Compare Moroccan Arabic بنين (bnīn), Libyan Arabic بنين (bnīn) and Tunisian Arabic بنين (bnīn).

parole.significato: gusset (small piece of cloth inserted in a garment)

parole.testo: Perhaps from a dialectal Arabic word for “stout, corpulent”. Compare Tunisian Arabic مبطبط (mbaṭbaṭ, “fat, fatso”). In line with this, Vassalli gives the form botbot (plural btabet). The similarity with Portuguese bode (“billygoat”) is suggestive, but the word seems to be restricted to the western h

From Arabic بَسْطة (basṭa, “width, ampleness, increase, excellence”), rarer also بُسْطة (busṭa). Additionally, Maltese bosta is the regular outcome of Arabic بُسَطاء (busaṭāʔ, “the common people, the uneducated crowd”); it is possible, though not necessary, that this etymon also contributed to the M

From Arabic, from the root ب ق ل (b q l). Related to بَقْل (baql, “vegetables, green plants, herbs”). Compare Moroccan Arabic بقولة (baqqūla, “spinach”), Andalusian Arabic رييس البقول (rayīs el-buqūl, “spinach”).

parole.significato: tepidness; coolness (lack of warmth, a neutral temperature)

parole.testo: From Arabic بَاذِنْجَان (bāḏinjān). The word shows a great variety of phonetic alterations among Arabic dialects. The same form as in Maltese appears to underly in Portuguese beringela.
From Arabic بِطَالَة (biṭāla, “work stoppage, free time, holiday”).
From Arabic أَبُو (ʔabū), construct state of أَب (ʔab, “father”).

Equivalent to Maghrebi Arabic بُوقال (būqāl), Sicilian bucali, Ancient Greek βαύκαλις (baúkalis), a wanderwort that seems to have been borrowed back and forth throughout the Mediterranean, though it is eventually thought to be of North African origin. The Maltese plural proves Sicilian influence, bu
From bu + qrajq, with qrajq diminutive form of obsolete qarq, from Arabic قَرْق (qarq, “clucking”).
From Arabic أَبُو رُكْبَة (ʔabū rukba, “kohlrabi”). By surface analysis, bu + rkoppa.

parole.significato: announcement, message, especially a positive one

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic مَشِيمَة (mašīma). Compare Tunisian Arabic بشيمة (bšīma).
From Arabic بُحَيْرَة (buḥayra). By surface analysis, diminutive of baħar. Compare Moroccan Arabic and Tunisian Arabic بحيرة (bḥīra, “vegetable garden, lake”).
Inherited from common Maghrebi Arabic, eventually from بِحالِ (bi-ḥāli, literally “in the state of”). Compare Moroccan Arabic بحال (bḥāl).

From Arabic أَبْزار (ʔabzār, “spice”). The specific sense “pepper” also in Moroccan Arabic بزار (bzār). Compare further the unrelated but similar-sounding Arabic بَهار (bahār, “spice”), whence North Levantine Arabic بهار (bhār, “pepper”).

parole.significato: to melt (become liquid, especially through warmth)

parole.testo: From Arabic دَعَا (daʕā, “to call, call upon God, pray”). The sense is from the construction دَعَا عَلَى (daʕā ʕalā, “to imprecate, pray for divine vengeance against”). The same generalisation in the sense of “to curse, swear, abuse” is found in some Arabic dialects, though only for the prepositiona
Agent noun of dagħa, from Arabic دَعَا (daʕā).

Derived from Arabic دَعَبَ (daʕaba, “to thrust, push”, and of wind or water “to be violent”). The sense “abyss” then probably from the violent currents at the bottom of a steep coast, transferred to the coast itself.

parole.significato: to overdo, to overload the mind

parole.testo: From Arabic دَغْمِيّ (daḡmiyy), from Arabic دَغْم (daḡm).

From Arabic ذَكَّرَ (ḏakkara, “to pollinate artificially”), derived from ذَكَر (ḏakar, “male”). The sense “influence” may be merely a figurative use of the former; compare for example English fertilize, German befruchten. However, it might also continue the sense “remind, admonish” of the Arabic ver
From Arabic ذَا الْوَقْت (ḏā al-waqt, “this time”). Compare Egyptian Arabic دِلْوَقْتِ (dilwa't).

parole.significato: to last; to take (time, especially long time)

parole.testo: From Arabic ذَا (ḏā, “this, that”). The paragogic -n probably spread from the plural, where it originated by analogy with hawn (“here”) and/or with the plural ending -in (compare Algerian Arabic هادون (hādūn) alongside هادو (hādū)). Some earlier scholars instead suspected a connection with Aramaic ד

parole.significato: beard in general, as a style

parole.testo: From Arabic دَقَّ (daqqa, “to knock”, dialectally also “play an instrument”).

parole.significato: as much as; to the degree of
parole.testo: Aquilina identifies it with Bedouin Tunisian Arabic تقز (tagz, “similar in age, height, weight, etc.”). Though this seems likely, it does not solve the question of eventual origin. Perhaps from underlying ta’ qies (literally “of measure”), from Arabic قَيْس (qays). The Tunisian -z must then be due t
From Arabic دَار (dār). Cognate with Sicilian dieri.

parole.significato: to turn; to veer; to change direction
to get used to (adapt to something new, make it customary)

parole.testo: Present participle of dara (“to get used to”). Diachronically from Arabic دَارٍ (dārin).
From Arabic ضِرْس (ḍirs), though properly perhaps a backformation from the plural, as also in nejba (“canine”). Compare Tunisian Arabic زرسة (zarsa), Moroccan Arabic ضرسة (ḍarsa).
From Arabic ضَوْء (ḍawʔ) with a paragogic -l, perhaps from a following article by resegmentation, and/or under influence of the antonym dell (“shade”).
Inherited from Arabic دَوْرَة (dawra). By surface analysis, dawr + -a. Doublet of dura.

parole.significato: to turn round, make round, make into a circle

parole.testo: Inherited, not from Arabic ضَحِكَ (ḍaḥika), which would yield *deħak, but rather a dialectal variant Arabic ضَحَكَ (ḍaḥaka).

parole.significato: to enter, come in, go in
a laughter (single instance of laughing; a way of laughing)
parole.testo: From Arabic ضَحْكة (ḍaḥka), singulative of ضَحْك (ḍaḥk).

parole.significato: to make laugh; to be funny
parole.testo: From Arabic ضَحَّكَ (ḍaḥḥaka), factitive second stem of ضَحِكَ (ḍaḥika), whence Maltese daħak (“to laugh”).
From a merger of Arabic تَضَيَّقَ (taḍayyaqa) and تَضايَقَ (taḍāyaqa), both from ضَيِّق (ḍayyiq, “narrow”).

parole.significato: to slaughter and sacrifice a victim (usually an animal)

parole.testo: From Arabic دَابَّة (dābba, “mount, beast of burden”).

parole.significato: an animal or human sacrifice; an instance of sacrificial slaughter
gold; golden (made of gold and/or of its colour)
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic ذَهَبِيّ (ḏahabiyy). By surface analysis, deheb + -i.

parole.significato: to appear; to become visible; to show up
parole.testo: From Arabic ظَهَرَ (ẓahara, “to appear”). The unexpected imala may be connected to an irregular development in some roots with final /r/, compare difer and sider. Compare also dahar (“back”), which shows the expected vocalism.
Inherited from Arabic ذِهْنِيّ (ḏihniyy). By surface analysis, dehen + -i.

From Arabic ضَيِّق (ḍayyiq). The expected form would be *dajjaq due to the originally emphatic ḍ (compare tajjeb). This influence was either levelled out in Maltese or the underlying form was a dissimilated variant dayyiq, ḏayyiq, which exists in several Arabic dialects.
From a merger of Arabic ضَيَّقَ (ḍayyaqa) and ضايَقَ (ḍāyaqa), both from etymology 1.

parole.significato: extremity, skirt (eg. of a mountain or a hill)
debt (money owed; the state of owing money)

parole.testo: From Arabic دَيْر (dayr, “convent, monastery”), from Classical Syriac ܕܝܪܐ (dayrā). The meaning “castle, fortress” perhaps influenced by the militant Order of Malta. The knowledge about the word’s origins seems to have been lost rather early, as Vassalli already treats the sense “convent” as seconda
Back-formation from the plural dmiel, from Arabic دَمَال (damāl, “dung”).

parole.significato: tear (drop of clear salty liquid from the eyes)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic دَامِلَة (dāmila). Compare Arabic دُمَّل (dummal, “ulcer”).
Inherited from Arabic دَم (dam), from Proto-Semitic *dam-, from Proto-Afroasiatic *dam-.

parole.significato: one who dungs, who uses manure

parole.testo: From Arabic دَامُوس (dāmūs), variant of دَيْمَاس (daymās).
Inherited from dialectal Arabic. Compare Iraqi Arabic دندل (dandal, “to hang, to dangle”). The Formal Arabic form is Arabic دَلْدَلَ (daldala, “to dangle”).
From a dialectal variant of Arabic دَرْفِيل (darfīl), دُلْفِين (dulfīn), which also underlies in Moroccan Arabic دنفيل (danfīl). Ultimately from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís).
From Arabic دَنِيء (danīʔ, “bad, evil, contemptible” and “weak, unable to partake of food”).

parole.significato: to thresh or winnow (separate the grain from the chaff, regardless of manner)
parole.testo: From Arabic ذَرَّى (ḏarrā), intensive of ذَرَا (ḏarā).
An irregular reflex from Arabic ضَرْو (ḍarw) (the expected one would be *daru).

parole.significato: to sound, to ring, to echo
to cure, treat, help (someone wounded or their wounds, someone ill or their issues)
to be full in worms or lice

parole.testo: From Arabic ضُعَيِّف (ḍuʕayyif), diminutive of ضَعِيف (ḍaʕīf), whence Maltese dgħif (“lean”).
Inherited from dialectal Arabic; compare Tunisian Arabic دغيسة (dḡīsa, “lightship”). Apparently a diminutive form.
From Arabic ضَعِيف (ḍaʕīf, “weak”). The original sense is continued by dgħajjef, from a diminutive.
Inherited from Arabic ذِئْب (ḏiʔb). Compare Moroccan Arabic ديب (dīb), Egyptian Arabic ديب (dīb).

parole.significato: pleasantly warm, but not too hot
to gild; to coat with or turn into gold

parole.testo: From Arabic ظُفْر (ẓufr). The unexpected imala may be connected to an irregular development in some roots with final /r/, compare deher and sider.
From Arabic دِيك (dīk, “rooster, cock”), with the feminine suffix -a.

parole.significato: bench made of stone or wood
parole.testo: From dialectal Arabic دُكَّانَة (dukkāna). Compare Moroccan Arabic and Algerian Arabic دكانة (dukkāna, “stone bench”).

parole.significato: to sin, to commit a sin
a small coin less than a ħabba
parole.testo: From Arabic دِينَار (dīnār). Aquilina suggests a derivation from Sicilian dinaru but it is unlikely because of the plural dwiener.
Possibly inherited from Arabic دُنْيَوِيّ (dunyawiyy), which in Maltese would have been bound to undergo either contraction or stress shift. Otherwise independently derived from dinja + -i.
Probably from Arabic ظِرْبَاء (ẓirbāʔ), a variant of ظَرِبَان (ẓaribān).
From Arabic ضَمِير (ḍamīr, “conscience”). The shift of meaning is probably due to the semantic influence of dovere (“duty”).

parole.significato: force used against someone; violence; sanction

parole.testo: From Arabic ذُنُوب (ḏunūb), plural of ذَنْب (ḏanb, “sin, sinful or blameworthy act, blame, moral guilt”). The Arabic plural was reanalysed as a singular, perhaps due to the notion, chiefly (though not exclusively) Christian, of sin as a continuing state, rather than only a repeatable act. For this “

From Arabic. Probably the imperfect of ظَنَّ (ẓanna, “to think, opine, conjecture”) in a phrase like أَظُنُّهُم مُتَضايِقِين (ʔaẓunnuhum mutaḍāyiqīn, “I think them despondent”). Then reconstrued as an adverb (or false verb). Alternatively from the related noun ظَنّ (ẓann, “opinion, conjecture”), but
Derived from dara, from Arabic دَرَى (darā).
Inherited from Arabic تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ (tisʕata ʕašara). By surface analysis, disat + -ax. Compare Egyptian Arabic تسعتاشر (tisʕatāšar).

parole.significato: watermelon (as a mass or species); several watermelons
a hut used by hunters and birdcatchers as a watching place
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic دَوْرَة (dawra). Doublet of dawra.

parole.significato: cure, remedy, help (to someone wounded or ill)

parole.testo: From Arabic آمَنَ (ʔāmana), a contracted fourth stem reconstrued as a second stem. This reconstruction may have happened at a later stage as the few inherited second stems with an initial vowel (or Arabic hamza) have i- in Maltese.

parole.significato: height, the worst or severest period (of something)
parole.testo: From underlying *eqlel, comparative (or elative) of archaic qlil (“ferocious”), itself probably from a merger of Arabic غَلِيل (ḡalīl) and قَلِيل (qalīl). For the development compare qilla.
Inherited from Arabic أَرْبَعَةَ عَشَرَ (ʔarbaʕata ʕašara). By surface analysis, erbat + -ax.
From Maghrebi Arabic أَرْخَة (ʔarḵa). Compare Tunisian Arabic أرخة (ʔarḵa).

parole.significato: the day before yesterday; two days ago
parole.testo: From Arabic أَوَّلَ أَمْس (ʔawwala ʔams). The long vowel is explainable as early contraction with the accusative ending -a, thus ʾawwala ʾams → ʾawwalām(i)s. A variant ʾāmis of Arabic أَمْس (ʔams) is apparently attested in isolated dialects, but it could also be due to backformation from the aforeme
From Arabic أَوَّلَانِيّ (ʔawwalāniyy), non-classical derivative from أَوَّل (ʔawwal, “first”), whence Maltese ewwel. By surface analysis, ewwel + -ieni.

parole.significato: first (of a series or order, before second and third)
to be left over, remain as a rest or surplus
to burst something; to cause to crack or explode
parole.testo: From Arabic فَقَعَ (faqaʕa), variant of فَجَعَ (fajaʕa).

parole.significato: to hatch (to emerge from an egg)
mushroom, mushrooms (several or a mass of them; the species as such)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic فَقُّوس الْحِمَار (faqqūs al-ḥimār).

parole.significato: relief, disburdenment; joy that dispels sorrow; comfort, solace
to brush off, to swipe away

parole.testo: From Arabic فَرَّكَ (farraka, “to rub forcefully, to grind”).

parole.significato: to care for someone in sorrow, illness, misery; to be there for; to comfort
parole.testo: From Arabic فَرَّجَ (farraja, “to allay someone's sorrow, relieve, disburden”).

parole.significato: to make bleed, e.g. by bloodletting
to have lunch, to eat lunch
to fill to the brim; to cause to overflow
parole.testo: From Arabic فَوَّرَ (fawwara, “to make boil”). The sense without doubt from “boiling over”.
Inherited from Arabic فَحْمِيّ (faḥmiyy). By surface analysis, faħam + -i.

parole.significato: obscenity, something outrageous, especially indecent talk
a type of Maltese pasta similar to tagliatelle
parole.testo: Dialectal Arabic فِدَاوِش (fidāwiš, “noodles”), which may be from Italian fettuccia (“band, ribbon”)

parole.significato: to redeem; to ransom; to deliver
parole.testo: From Arabic فَدَى (fadā), which is also used in the Christian religious sense. The financial sense is probably a loan translation of or at least influenced by English redeem. Unrelated with borrowed fada (“to trust”).
Singulative derivation from Arabic فَهْم (fahm, “understanding”). Verbal noun of fehem (“to understand”).

Inherited from Arabic فِي أَيْنَ (fī ʔayna). By surface analysis, f’ + *ejn. Compare Tunisian Arabic فين (fīn/fāyn), Moroccan Arabic فين (fīn), فاين (fāyin), Hijazi Arabic فين (fēn) and Egyptian Arabic فين (fēn).
From Arabic فَيْجَل (fayjal), variant of فَيْجَن (fayjan), from Aramaic פיגנא (peygānā), from Ancient Greek πήγανον (pḗganon).
Inherited from Maghrebi Arabic, from a Berber language. Compare Tunisian Arabic فكرون (fakrūn), Moroccan Arabic فكرون (fakrūn).
From Arabic فَلَى (falā, “to louse, inspect someone’s head for lice”).

parole.significato: to be able to afford, endure, or withstand

parole.testo: Inherited from dialectal Maghrebi Arabic (compare Tunisian Arabic فَلّوس (fallūs), Libyan Arabic فِلُّوس (fillūs), Moroccan Arabic فلوس (fallūs)), from a Berber language, from Latin pullus.

parole.significato: foal, colt (a preadult horse or ass which has been weaned)
to exhaust (somebody), to tire out (especially spiritually)
to pass through something, to split, part, e.g. the sea (of a boat), a crowd (of a person), hair (of a comb)

parole.testo: Extension of fergħ, from Arabic فَرْع (farʕ). The original form has become rare as it is homophonous with ferħ (“joy” and “young animal”).
From Arabic فِرْعَوْن (firʕawn, “pharaoh”). The tyranny of the pharaohs, especially with regard to Moses, is very much stressed in the Quran and has become proverbial in Arabic. Doublet of fargħun.
A denominal verb from Maghrebi Arabic فَرْنَق (farnaq, “furnace”), from Latin fornāx.

parole.significato: to interpose (to intervene in a dispute, or in a conversation)
to spread out; to spread something over a surface
a young animal, especially a kitten
parole.testo: From Arabic فَرْخ (farḵ, “chick”, formerly also “young of any animal”).

From Arabic وَسْوَسَ (waswasa). The replacement of /w/ with voiceless /f/ is onomatopoeic; moreover it simplifies the formation of the conjugated forms since forms like weswsu would have to be contracted (compare werwer).

parole.significato: to unstitch, unseam, rip the seam of

parole.testo: From dialectal Arabic. Compare Moroccan Arabic تفتف (taftaf, “to stutter”).

parole.significato: to unstitch, unseam, rip the seam of

parole.testo: Probably from Arabic فَجَأَ (fajaʔa, “to appear suddenly”). The phonetic form is slightly irregular (as one would expect *feġa) however its possible it was influenced by the event noun feġġ formed from the instance noun feġġa from Arabic فَجْأة (fajʔa). Alternatively perhaps from فَجَّ (fajja) with
From Arabic أَفْعَال (ʔafʕāl), plural of فِعْل (fiʕl).

parole.significato: to separate people from one another
lukewarm; tepid (having a temperature close to room temperature or human body temperature)
parole.testo: From Arabic فَاتِر (fātir) with r/l-variation as fairly often in Maltese.
From Arabic فِي أَيِّ شَيْء (fī ʔayyi šayʔ, “in what thing”). By surface analysis, f’ + *iex. Compare Moroccan Arabic فاش (fāš).

parole.significato: to have a good smell, scent, be fragrant

parole.testo: From Arabic فِي الْمِئَة (fī l-miʔa, literally “in the hundred”).

parole.significato: to paralyse, cause to become paralysed
parole.testo: From Arabic فَلَجَ (falaja, “to paralyse”, chiefly in the passive).
From fil-għaxija (literally “in the evening”), from Arabic عَشِيّة (ʕašiyya).
From Arabic فِي الْغُدُوِّ (fī l-ḡuduwwi), from غُدُوّ (ḡuduww, “morning time”).

parole.significato: to spread out, to spread something over a surface

parole.testo: From Arabic فِي سَاعَة (fī sāʕa, “in a short time”). Compare Moroccan Arabic فيساع (fīsāʕ).

parole.significato: to spoil; to pamper; to be indulgent with
parole.testo: Second stem replacing Arabic أَفْسَدَ (ʔafsada, “to corrupt, make decadent”).

parole.significato: to mean; to have a meaning
to search; to seek; to look for
so-and-so, that bloke; a placeholder for a person whose name one cannot or does not want to mention, as in the phrase;…

parole.testo: From underlying fl-mkien (“in the place, on the spot”), from Arabic فِي الْمَكان (fī al-makān). Probably from such collocations as ilkoll flimkien, originally “everybody in the place” and hence “all those present together”.
From Arabic فَم (fam). Cognate with Moroccan Arabic فم (fumm).
Inherited from Arabic فُنْدُق (funduq), borrowed from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον (pandokeîon).

From Arabic فُرْن (furn), from Aramaic פורנא / ܦܘܪܢܐ (pūrnā), from Ancient Greek φοῦρνος (phoûrnos), from Latin furnus. There is no reason to doubt the inheritance of the word in Maltese and consider it a borrowing from an Italo-Romance cognate such as Italian forno. The Arabic word is attested earl
From f’ + wast (now obsolete), from Arabic فِي وَسْط (fī wasṭ, “in middle [of]”).
From the Arabic root ف ر ك (f r k). Perhaps originally from a plural *أَفْراك (*ʔafrāk).
From Maghrebi Arabic فُرَار (furār), ultimately from Latin Februārius.
Extended form of frugħ, from Arabic فُرُوغ (furūḡ).
From Arabic فَساد (fasād, “corruption, decadence”) and/or إفْساد (ʔifsād, “the act of corrupting, making decadent”). Both forms would have merged phonetically in Maltese.
From Arabic اِفْتَخَرَ (iftaḵara, “to be proud, to boast”).

parole.significato: to agree (among each other); to reach an agreement or deal
parole.testo: From Arabic تَفاهَمَ (tafāhama) with metathesis and reanalysis as an eighth stem.

parole.significato: a kind of flat, usually ring-shaped bread, often used for sandwiches
on; upon (at the top, on the surface of)
parole.testo: From Arabic فَوْقَ (fawqa, preposition), فَوْقُ (fawqu, adverb). The Arabic words mean only “over, above”, but the Maltese preposition gained additional senses from għal (now only “for, to”).
From the older wistani, from Arabic وَسْطانِيّ (wasṭāniyy), altered after related fost (“among”), which see. By surface analysis, fost + -ani.

parole.significato: a piece of cloth kept at hand for wiping one’s hands during work

parole.testo: From Arabic يَمَام (yamām), also pronounced جَمَام (jamām) dialectally. For the shift from /d͡ʒ/ to /ɡ/, compare Moroccan Arabic جربوع (jarbūʕ), ݣربوع (garbūʕ).
From Arabic كَرَّ (karra, “make a rattling or gurgling sound”).
From an extension of the Arabic root ك ر ب (k r b).
Probably related to فركش (“to trip”). Otherwise from Arabic خَرْفَشَ (ḵarfaša) or a variant of it.
Intensive of a dialectal Arabic كَرَش (karaš, “to drive away”), which is attested in Egypt, Saudi Arabia and parts of the Levant.
From Maghrebi Arabic, from a Berber language. Compare Libyan Arabic قرجومة (garjūma), Moroccan Arabic قرجوطة (qarjūṭa).
Possibly related to Arabic جزر (jazara) (in the sense to 'wrap what was slaughtered').

parole.significato: to accuse or tell that something is false

parole.testo: From Arabic كَذَبَ (kaḏaba). The shift [kd] → [ɡd] is a regular assimilation, but the [ɡ] was then irregularly generalised throughout the root.
From Arabic كَدَمَ (kadama, “to bite, bite off”) with g- by generalisation of regular assimilation in the inflected forms (as also in gideb).

From Arabic كُدْس (kuds, “to pile”). In the original plural أَكْداس (ʔakdās) and in certain forms of the related verb كَدَسَ (kadasa), the -k- was voiced by assimilation to the following -d-, and this voicing was then generalised (as in gideb, gidem etc.). In a second step the cluster -ds- was reana

Uncertain. An earlier proposal derives the term from Arabic دَرَمَ (darama, “to run with short steps (said of a hare or hedgehog)”) + شَوِل (šawil), شَوْل (šawl, “agile, swift”), though such verb-adjective compounds are not a typical means of noun formation in Arabic. Inherited from Arabic كُدْيَة (kudya), with an irregular lengthening of the first vowel and voicing of /k/ due to the following /d/. Compare Moroccan Arabic كدية (kudya, “hill”).

parole.significato: to adore, to worship, to serve
to load (put something on a means of transportation)
sunset, dusk, twilight (period between daylight and darkness)

parole.testo: From Arabic عَبِيد (ʕabīd), plural of عَبْد (ʕabd).

From Arabic عَادَ (ʕāda, “he returned, did again”). Compare مَا عادَ (mā ʕāda, “he stopped, did no more”), which has also become an adverb in many dialects and may be construed with pronominal suffixes in some of them. Compare Moroccan Arabic عاد (ʕād) and Hebrew עוד (ʿōd, “still”).

parole.significato: only used in għad li (“it is said that”)
parole.testo: From Arabic أَعَادَ (ʔaʕāda, “to repeat, say repeatedly”).
From Arabic غَدًا (ḡadan). Most Arabic dialects have replaced the word with بُكْرة (bukra, “[in the] morning”), but Maghrebi dialects, to which Maltese is closely related, have preserved it.

parole.significato: several bones; bone as a material
to pass on; to hand down

parole.testo: From Arabic عَذَّبَ (ʕaḏḏaba). In several conjugated forms the verb ultimately merged with għaddab (“to anger”), which facilitated its deplacement.
Inherited from Arabic عَدُوّ (ʕaduww). The plural għedewwa continues Arabic عَداوة (ʕadāwa, “enmity”), reinterpreted as plural by analogy with forms like qraba, Nsara.
Intensive second stem of Arabic عَفِجَ (ʕafija, “to beat”).

From Arabic غَاغَة (ḡāḡa, “mob, crowd”). The word is an extreme example of how the loss/vowelisation of għ has weakened the phonetic shapes of many words in Maltese. One might think that għagħa would subsequently have come out of use, but it remains common.
Derived verbal noun of form I verb għad (to say, to tell), itself from form IV Arabic أَعَادَ (ʔaʕāda, “to repeat, say repeatedly”). For the form, compare għajnuna.

Derived verbal noun of form I verb għad (to say, to tell), itself from form IV Arabic أَعَادَ (ʔaʕāda, “to repeat, say repeatedly”). Compare Arabic عَوْدَات (ʕawdāt), plural of عَوْدَة (ʕawda), derived verbal noun of form I verb عَادَ (ʕāda⁩). For the form compare also għajnuna.
From Arabic عَيَّرَ (ʕayyara, “to put to shame”).
Inherited from Arabic عَيَّطَ (ʕayyaṭa). Cognate with Tunisian Arabic عَيِّط (ʕayyeṭ)

parole.significato: to curse by means of the evil eye
parole.testo: From Arabic عَيَّنَ (ʕayyana) and/or عايَنَ (ʕāyana). Both would have merged in Maltese.

parole.significato: plum, plums (several fruits; plum as a mass, taste, species)
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic عَيْن بَقَر (ʕayn baqar). By surface analysis, għajn + baqar.
Derived from għen, itself from Arabic أَعانَ (ʔaʕāna). Compare Arabic مَعُونة (maʕūna). For the form compare also دَيْنُونة (daynūna) and suchlike.
From Arabic عَيْش (ʕayš), perhaps merged with عِيشة (ʕīša).
Derived from għex, from Arabic عَاشَ (ʕāša).

The basic sense of the Maltese root is “being weak, feeble, deprived”, which is most readily derived from Arabic عَجْز (ʕajz) and its root; compare għaks (“oppression, destitution, famine”). Phonetically this is plausible since Arabic ج (j) becomes Maltese g in several words, especially in the vicin
Perhaps from Arabic عَجُز (ʕajuz, “buttocks; hindlegs; rear of anything”). For the phonetics compare the argumentation at għakkes.

parole.significato: suddenly, at once, unexpectedly, without warning
parole.testo: From Arabic عَلَى غَيْرِ إرادَة (ʕalā ḡayri ʔirāda, “involuntarily”). By surface analysis, għal + għajr + rieda. The development from “involuntarily” to “unexpectedly” is semantically straightforward. Theories that connect the expression with Arabic عَرَض (ʕaraḍ, “unexpected event, accident”) are ru
From Arabic غَلَقَ (ḡalaqa), أَغْلَقَ (ʔaḡlaqa). * Homophone: agħlaq (except rural) * Rhymes: -alaʔ, -aːlaʔ, -aˤːlaʔ

From underlying Arabic عَلَى أَيِّ شَيْء (ʕalā ʔayyi šayʔ, literally “on what thing”). By surface analysis, għal (“for”) + *iex (“what”); see xiex for the latter. Cognate with Moroccan Arabic علاش (ʕlāš, “why”).

parole.significato: to boil (a liquid); to cause to boil; to cook by boiling
parole.testo: From Arabic غَلَّى (ḡallā), causative of غَلَى (ḡalā), يَغْلِي (yaḡlī), whence Maltese għela (“to boil, be boiled”).

parole.significato: to raise the price of; to make something more expensive
parole.testo: From Arabic غَلَّى (ḡallā), causative of غَلَا (ḡalā), يَغْلُو (yaḡlū), whence Maltese għela (“to rise in price”).

parole.significato: to kill by hanging; to hang

parole.testo: From the Arabic root غ ل ق (ḡ l q). The sense “enclosure, fenced or immured area” was still attested in older Maltese. The phonetic similarity with Arabic حَقْل (ḥaql) is coincidental.
From Arabic عَمًى (ʕaman, “blindness”). Originally a masculine, but feminine in Maltese due to the final -a and hence distinguishable from the adjective (etymology 3 below).

parole.significato: to blind, to make someone blind

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic عَمِلَ (ʕamila). Cognate with Tunisian Arabic عمَل (ʕmal)

parole.significato: to dip (to lower into a liquid)
depth (that which is deep below; the deepest part)
parole.testo: Probably from Arabic أَعْماق (ʔaʕmāq, “depths”), plural of عُمْق (ʕumq). Alternatively from the nominalised adjective عَمِيق (ʕamīq, “deep”), or from a blend of them. The forms would have merged phonetically in Maltese. Compare għammieq.

parole.significato: to dip (to lower into a liquid)
to dazzle (blind temporarily through excessive light)
parole.testo: Factitive derivation from Arabic عَمِشَ (ʕamiša, “to be bleary- or watery-eyed, to have reduced sight”).

Going by the spelling, from an underlying Arabic *عَمّاق (*ʕammāq), which would seem to be an intensive form of عَمِيق (ʕamīq, “deep”). However, given the vocalic mergers involving għ and q in Maltese, the root would have been liable to irregular developments. Compare għamieq (“depth”) for more.

parole.significato: livestock, cattle (in the broader sense), especially sheep
a young goat (at roughly one year of age)

parole.testo: From Arabic عَنَّقَ (ʕannaqa), عانَقَ (ʕānaqa), from عُنُق (ʕunuq, “neck”), whence Maltese għonq.

parole.significato: to coagulate; to congeal; to become thick

parole.testo: From Arabic عَقَبَة (ʕaqaba, “mountain pass, steep ascent, obstacle”).

parole.significato: union (institution or commitment by which two or more persons become united, e.g. marriage)
parole.testo: Singulative derivation from Arabic عَقْد (ʕaqd, “tying, binding, contracting”).
Inherited from Arabic عَقْلِيّ (ʕaqliyy). By surface analysis, għaqal + -i.

parole.significato: to join together; to unite; to unify
parole.testo: From Arabic عَقَّدَ (ʕaqqada), intensive second stem of عَقَدَ (ʕaqada).

From Arabic عَلَى ٱلرِّيقِ (ʕala r-rīqi, “on an empty stomach”). Equivalent to għal (“on”) + ir-riq (“the saliva”), literally “on the saliva”. Compare Moroccan Arabic عالريق (ʕar-rīq) and Egyptian Arabic عالرايق (ʕar-rāyeʔ).

parole.significato: to recognise, become aware of, find out
parole.testo: From Arabic عَرَفَ (ʕarafa). Doublet of the contracted imperfect jaf (“to know”).

From Arabic عَرَبِيّ (ʕarabiyy). One of the few words referring to Arabo-Islamic culture that was actually inherited (and not later reborrowed from Italian). Might also be used to refer to the early forms of Maltese language either by its speakers or foreigners who visited Muslim and later re-Christ
From Arabic عَارِف (ʕārif), active participle of عَرَفَ (ʕarafa, “to know”), whence Maltese jaf and għaraf.
From Arabic غَرْغَرَ (ḡarḡara, “to gurgle”), of onomatopoetic origin.
From Arabic عَرْعار (ʕarʕār), variant of عَرْعَر (ʕarʕar, “juniper”).
From Arabic عَرِيش (ʕarīš, “simple structure, shed, shelter”).

From Arabic عَرَّشَ (ʕarraša). The sense “to become overcast” from the use of għarix for a shade-giving tent or awning. The sense “to peer” is less straightforward. Possibly from the idea that someone on the lookout would build themselves such a tent. Or perhaps in the sense of English to shadow, Ge

From Arabic عَرُوس (ʿarūs, usually “bride”, but also “bridegroom”). Used the same way in city dialects of Tunisia. Possibly in part a backformation from the marked feminine għarusa, from Arabic عَرُوسة (ʕarūsa, “bride”). The commoner Arabic word for “bridegroom” is عَرِيس (ʕarīs).
From Arabic عُرْيان (ʕuryān, “naked”) with irregular -w- instead of -j-.

Inherited from Arabic عَصْر (ʕaṣr). The religious use is based on the Islamic afternoon prayer. Catholic vespers are typically held at 6 pm, but were often brought forward to the last hour before sunset during the winter. The word counts among the specifically Islamic terms preserved by the (re-)con
Inherited from Arabic عَسَلِيّ (ʕasaliyy). By surface analysis, għasel + -i.
From Arabic. Compare Moroccan Arabic عسري (ʕasri, “left-handed”).
From Arabic عَسَّة (ʕassa, “guard”). Compare Moroccan Arabic عسة (ʕassa).
Intensive form of għass, from Arabic عَسَّ (ʕassa).

parole.significato: to (try to) conceal something that is bound to come out
parole.testo: From Arabic غَطَّى الشَّمْسَ بِالْغِرْبالِ (ḡaṭṭā š-šamsa bi-l-ḡirbāli, literally “to cover the sun with a sieve”). Probably the idea is that the light of the sun could not be veiled even with an unperforated surface, but with a sieve the attempt is all the more hopeless. Compare Portuguese tapar o

parole.significato: to squash; to crush; to thump
parole.testo: In all likelihood from Arabic. Barring irregular phonetic developments, the only possible etymon seems to be عَطَّنَ (ʕaṭṭana, “to steep skin in a septic liquid for tanning”). Semantically, this is plausible through figurative use; compare e.g. English tan, Latin macerare, older German gerben.
Inherited from Arabic عَتُّوقَة (ʕattūqa). Compare Tunisian Arabic عتوقة (ʕattūqa, “pullet”), Algerian Arabic عتوقة (ʕattūqa, “pullet”), Moroccan Arabic عتوقة (ʕattūqa, “pullet; young girl”).
From Arabic غِطَاء (ḡiṭāʔ). However, the final -u is hardly explainable from this form; hence probably merged with غَطْو (ḡaṭw, “the act of covering”).

parole.significato: to make something float, make someone swim

parole.testo: From Arabic عَلَى شَأْنِ (ʕalā šaʔni, literally “on the issue of”) or a contraction of għaliex. Cognate with Egyptian Arabic عشان, علشان (ʕašān, ʕalašān, “because”). Compare also Maltese biex.

parole.significato: to hurry; to be quick or hasty
to comfort (someone) in times of mourning, to offer condolences, to console, to declare regret for someone's loss
a disused Maltese custom where neighbors cooked a meal for a grieving family, who refrained from cooking to avoid worse…
to dig (a field) over, to hoe

parole.testo: From Arabic عَزَلَ (ʕazala, “to isolate, set aside”). Compare Moroccan Arabic عزل (ʕzal, “to choose, to select; to separate”).
Inherited from Arabic عَزِيز (ʕazīz). Doublet of żżiżża.

From Arabic عَجْز (ʕajz). The sense “laziness” is also found in several dialects. Compare further għaks (“destitution, famine”), which might be a doublet of this (with dissimilation, rather than assimilation as in għażż).

parole.significato: to offer condolences, to console, to declare regret for someone's loss

parole.testo: From Arabic غَزْغَزَ (ḡazḡaza), غَزَّزَ (ḡazzaza). Compare Moroccan Arabic غزز (ḡazzaz).

From Arabic غَزَالَة (ḡazāla, “female gazelle”). The survival of this word in Malta is perhaps due its frequent figurative and poetic use among the Arabs. The gemination may be due to influence by Italian gazzella, though it is also explainable through analogy.
Inherited from dialectal Arabic عَجْزان (ʕajzān). Compare Moroccan Arabic عجزان (ʕagzān).
Inherited from Arabic أَعْيَا (ʔaʕyā). Cognate with Tunisian Arabic عيِا (ʕye)

parole.significato: to rise in price; to become expensive
parole.testo: From Arabic غَلَا (ḡalā), يَغْلُو (yaḡlū, “to rise in price”).

parole.significato: to overcome, to defeat, to win out over
to make a mistake, to err

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic عَلَم (ʕalam), perhaps influenced by etymology 2, as one would expect *għalm or *għalem.

parole.significato: to be jealous of; to envy

parole.testo: From Arabic عَراء (ʕarāʔ), feminised because of the final -a.
Derived from għaraf, from Arabic عَرَفَ (ʕarafa, “to know”).
Derived from għarus, from Arabic عَرُوس (ʕarūs), with the common measure for abstract nouns.

parole.significato: the quality of being amazing, astonishing, surprising
parole.testo: Possibly an extended form of Arabic أُعْجُوبة (ʔuʕjūba, “wonder”). Otherwise derived from the root with the Maltese abstract-noun measure.
Inherited from Arabic عِيد الْخَمْسِين (ʕīd al-ḵamsīn). By surface analysis, għid + il- + ħamsin, literally “festival of the fifty”.

From Arabic غَيْرة (ḡayra, “jealousy, jealous zeal”), widely also pronounced غِيرة (ḡīra) in dialects, which is the underlying form in Maltese (the modern diphthong being due to the influence of the għ).
From Arabic غَطَسَ (ḡaṭasa) with irregular voicing of the second radical.

parole.significato: to ascend; to rise; to soar; to climb up (move to a higher position)
parole.testo: From Arabic عَلِيَ (ʕaliya, “to rise”). The sense “rise in price” was transferred from għela, from the originally unrelated Arabic غَلَا (ḡalā).

From Arabic عالِي (ʕālī, “high”). The irregular -o- probably from a merger with عُلْيَا (ʕulyā), feminine of أَعْلَى (ʔaʕlā, “higher, very high”), elative of the first-mentioned adjective. Because of this development, homophony with għali (“expensive”), from Arabic غالِي (ḡālī), was avoided; be it t

parole.significato: to raise; to lift (move something to a higher position)
parole.testo: From Arabic عَلَّى (ʕallā, “to raise”). The sense “raise the price of” was transferred from għalla, from the originally unrelated Arabic غَلَّى (ḡallā).
From Arabic عُلَّيْق (ʕullayq). Accordingly the more etymological spelling would seem to be (nonstandard) għolliq. The vowel phonemes /iː/ and /ɪː/ are merged before [ħ] and [ʔ].

parole.significato: lifespan, lifetime (the entire time of a person’s life; with regard to living persons also: that which has passed of it…

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic عُقَدِيّ (ʕuqadiyy). By surface analysis, għoqod + -i.
Inherited from Arabic عُصْفُرِيّ (ʕuṣfuriyy). By surface analysis, għosfor + -i.

Without doubt influenced by etymology 1 through evident analogies of both appearance and function, but originally perhaps from Arabic عُسّ (ʕuss), meaning “genitals” (especially male, but also female) as well as “large cup” (if this is the same word). Compare the obsolete Maltese variant għoss (“but

parole.significato: to please; to appeal to (often expresses English like)

parole.testo: From Arabic عِزّة (ʕizza, “prestige, standing, honour”). While the Arabic word refers to a quality of them who are cherished, the Maltese is subtly different in that it denotes the attitude with which others cherish them.

Singulative of Arabic عُود (ʕūd). The basic word was displaced by Maltese injam and is now only reserved for specifically hardwoods, as used by the similies iebes għuda and xieref għuda (as stiff/tough as hardwood).
From Arabic غُول (ḡūl). Cognate with English ghoul.

From Arabic جَزِيرَة (jazīra). The affrication of the initial consonant was blocked, or early on reverted, under the influence of the following alveolar fricative. Compare Moroccan Arabic جزيرة (gzīra).
From Arabic هَاهُنَا (hāhunā), emphatic form of هُنَا (hunā). Compare Sfaxi Tunisian Arabic هَون (hawn) and North Levantine Arabic هون (hawn, hōn).
From Arabic هَدَأَ (hadaʔa). One of the few extant verbs with initial h- that are not geminated (Arabic stems II or V); compare hemeż.

parole.significato: to calm someone down; to cause to relax
to fasten; to attach; to pin
parole.testo: From Arabic هَمَزَ (hamaza, “to squeeze, prick, prod, spur”). Originally “to pin” in Maltese, then generalised. Compare the noun hemża (“needle stich”) recorded in Vassalli’s dictionary.
Inherited from Arabic ثَمَّ (ṯamma). Compare Tunisian Arabic فمة (famma, “there is”) and Moroccan Arabic تم (tamm), تمة (tamma, “there”).

parole.significato: to wear out; to cause to deteriorate gradually

parole.testo: Perhaps an extended form of Arabic هَوَّدَ (hawwada), which originally means “to make or be gentle, slow, languid” and thence “to murmur, make demonic insinuations” as well as “to make drunk and sleepy”. The Maltese verb apparently has an archaic sense “to go mad, rave”, which can be derived from th

From Arabic هانِئ (hāniʔ, “happy”). The spelling with h instead of ħ is due to the fact that the Maltese root shows a mixed treatment of the onset. While hieni is usually pronounced with /ħ/, the noun hena is /ˈɛːna/, and the verbs henna, thenna allow both ways.
From Arabic هُنَا (hunā, “here”) or a related form. Compare hawn.
Inherited from Arabic هُمْ (hum). Compare Moroccan Arabic هوما (hūma), Egyptian Arabic هما (humma).
From Arabic أَبْهَم (ʔabham). Sense 3 is derived from bhima.

parole.significato: of a color between white and black

parole.testo: From general dialectal Arabic ايد (ʔīd), variant of classical يَد (yad). Doublet of jedd.
According to Aquilina, originally an VIII-form *itda, from Arabic ضَاءَ (ḍāʔa, “to shine”).
From Arabic أَذَّنَ (ʔaḏḏana, “to call to prayer; to crow”).
From Arabic يَابِس (yābis). The initial /j/ was lost. Irregularities involving this consonant in initial position are common; compare jiena, jew with unetymological j-.
From Arabic أَيُّ شَيْء (ʔayyu šayʔ, literally “what thing”). Cognate with Moroccan Arabic آش (ʔāš) and Hijazi Arabic إيش (ʔēš)

Inherited from Arabic آخَر (ʔāḵar). Compare Hebrew אחר (ʾaḥēr). The plural oħrajn is unusual in that the plural ending -in seems to have been added to the feminine ending (rather than replacing it as *oħrin). This might have to do with the fact that -a here goes back to Arabic long -ā, provided that
Alteration of Arabic كَرِيه (karīh, “hateful, ugly”) by analogy with other Color and defect adjectives.
From Arabic أَكْحَل (ʔakḥal, “black, very dark grey or blue, the colour of kohl”).
From Arabic مَاء (māʔ), with fused definite article.

parole.significato: Expresses the time that something has been going on; takes personal suffixes according to subject of the phrase and is…
parole.testo: Originally an alternative form of lilu (“to him”), etc., pronominal forms of Arabic لَ (la, “to, for”), إلَى (ʔilā, “to, towards”). The adverbial construction exists in several Arabic dialects; compare e.g. North Levantine Arabic إلي يومين ما نمت (ʔili yawmayn ma nimt, “I haven’t slept in two days”)
From Arabic أَمَّا (ʔammā, “as for, as regards, but”).
Probably from an underlying Arabic إن كانَ لَا (ʔin kāna lā, “if it were not so”, literally “if it were no”).

parole.significato: you (second-person singular subject pronoun) (generally distinguished as being feminine version of int)
peace be upon you (mostly used during Catholic masses by priests to greet)
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ (as-salāmu ʕalaykum, “peace be upon you”).

parole.significato: brown-skinned; tan; suntanned (having a skin colour that is relatively dark by standards of the Mediterranean, whether…

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic أُسْقُفِيَّة (ʔusqufiyya). By surface analysis, isqof + -ija.

Inherited from Arabic أُسْقُف (ʔusquf). One of the specifically Christian words in Maltese that were inherited from Arabic, suggesting that there were Arabic-speaking Christians in Malta during the Islamic reign. Otherwise, the words must have been brought in by missionaries during the re-Christiani

Contraction of is-siegħa (“[at] the hour”), from Arabic اَلسّاعة (as-sāʕa). Compare Iraqi Arabic هسا (hassa, “now”), Egyptian Arabic لسا (lissa, “still”),Tunisian Arabic السّاعة (ssêʕə, “for now, for the time being”).

From Arabic إِي وَ (ʔī wa-, “yes, by...”), which is to be followed by someone or something to swear by. Common combinations are, for example, إِي وَٱللّٰه (ʔī wa-llāh, “yes, by God”) or إِي وَرَبِّي (ʔī wa-rabbī, “yes, by my Lord”). Eventually the following word was left out. Compare the same in Hij

Uncertain. Perhaps from Arabic أَصْدَق (ʔaṣdaq, “more truthfully”, in the sense of “rather, more properly”). As the emphatic -ṣ- could have been assimilated to the -d- and/or dissimilated against the -q-, the form is entirely regular but for the loss of the final consonant. This loss in turn seems p

From Arabic جَزَى (jazā, “to requite”). The imperfect tense shows assimilation *niġżi → niżżi. The rare perfect is a backformation from the imperfect on the model of such a verb as idda. Doublet of ġeża ("to reward").

parole.significato: to know; to be able to do sth.
parole.testo: From Arabic يَعْرِفُ (yaʕrifu), imperfect of عَرَفَ (ʕarafa, “to know, get to know, find out”). Doublet of uncontracted għaraf (“to recognise, become aware of, find out”).

parole.significato: Followed by an imperfect verb, it expresses the optative, i.e. a wish or request.
parole.testo: From Arabic يَاٱللَّٰه (yāllāh). By surface analysis, ja + Alla, literally “O God!”.

parole.significato: to need, to use for some purpose
parole.testo: In all likelihood from a contraction of jagħmel bi, from the imperfect tense of Arabic عَمِلَ بِ (ʕamila bi, “to do with”), as in “What are you going to do with that?” Similar contractions compare in jaf (“to know”) and ġab (“to bring”). Another theory derives it from Arabic أَبَّ (ʔabba, “to wish,
From Maghrebi Arabic يَنَّار (yannār), ultimately from Latin Iānuārius.

From Arabic يَد (yad, “authority”, literally “hand”). Compare Latin manus, which may have influenced the semantic development. Doublet of id (“hand”), which continues the common dialectal Arabic form, while jedd was a more formal word that appeared in the classical shape.

Uncertain. Possibly from Arabic إِنْ كَانَ (ʔin kāna, “if be”) or Arabic يَكُون (yakūn, “to be”). Otherwise from Arabic إِنْ كَـ (ʔin ka-, “if as”). Compare Moroccan Arabic ياك (yāk) and Tunisian Arabic كان (kēn).

Unknown. Aquilina rejects a derivation from Arabic يَا سَلام (yā salām). The required contraction of sliem into -ssu is indeed unlikely. However, Aquilina’s own connection with Arabic يَسَّ (yassa, “to journey”) seems even less plausible. The phrase is reminiscent of dialectal Arabic الله عَلَيْك (a
Equivalent to Arabic أَوْ إلَّا (ʔaw ʔillā, literally “or other than”), as if saying “perhaps A, and otherwise perhaps B”.

From Arabic أَنَا (ʔanā) with expressive lengthening of the first syllable (*ʾānā) as generally in Maghrebi dialects; compare Tunisian Arabic آنا (ʔāna), Moroccan Arabic آنا (ʔāna). Eventually from Proto-Semitic *ʔanāku. Prefixed j- occurs more often in Maltese (compare jew); in this case perhaps ge

parole.significato: hope; but chiefly in a negative context, especially with qata’ (“to give up”)
a traditional kind of sweet pastry, usually ring-shaped
parole.testo: From Arabic كَعْك (kaʕk). The similarity with English cake is coincidental (or if anything due to highly remote relation).
From Arabic كَبَّار (kabbār), later influenced by Sicilian chiàppara and/or Italian cappero.
From Arabic كَرْفَأَة (karfaʔa). Compare Kabyle akerfa (“chaff”).

By back-formation from the plural krafes, from a variant of Arabic كَرَفْس (karafs) reinterpreted as a plural form. Compare Moroccan Arabic كرافس (krāfis, “celery”), Tunisian Arabic كرافس (krāfis, “celery”).
Inherited from Arabic كَرِيم (karīm, “kind, honourable, noble, generous”).
From dialectal Maghrebi Arabic كَرْكَر (karkar), reduplication of كَرّ (karr, “to drag”), itself possibly a variant of Classical جَرَّ (jarra) or influenced by it; compare Maltese ġarr.
From Maghrebi Arabic, from كَرْم (karm, “orchard”). Compare Tunisian Arabic كرموس (karmūs)، Moroccan Arabic كرموس (karmūs).
From Arabic كَشْكَشَ (kaškaša), influenced by karkar.

parole.significato: bluish; tinted in blue (of something not always blue, especially the sea and sky)
parole.testo: Derived from ikħal, from Arabic أَكْحَل (ʔakḥal).

Probably a backformation from kburija (“pride”), itself probably an alteration of Arabic كِبْرِياء (kibriyāʔ) after the common Maltese measure for abstract nouns (or otherwise an independent derivation from kbir with this measure).
Probably an alteration of Arabic كِبْرِياء (kibriyāʔ) after the common Maltese measure for abstract nouns, or otherwise an independent derivation from kbir with this measure.
Second stem replacing Arabic أَقْبَسَ (ʔaqbasa), with sporadic -k- for -q-.

parole.significato: palm of the hand; or the inner part of the hand (including the fingers)
to shroud, wrap in a shroud

parole.testo: Regarding the obsolete variant probably inherited from Arabic كُفْرِيّة (kufriyya, “blasphemousness, a blasphemy, an act of unbelief”). Alternatively formed from the adjective kiefer, from Arabic كافِر (kāfir), + -ija.

parole.significato: a unit of surface area that is officially 22.41 imperial square yards (18.74 m2).

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic كَلْبِيّ (kalbiyy). By surface analysis, kelb + -i.
From Arabic كَمُّون حُلْو (kammūn ḥulw). kemmun + ħelu.
From Arabic كِراء (kirāʔ), feminised because of the final -a. Doublet of kiri.

parole.significato: existence, being (the state or fact of existing)

parole.testo: Probably a reduplicated form of Arabic كَشَّ (kašša).

parole.significato: to grow (in general, e.g. children, plants, knowledge, etc.)

parole.testo: From Arabic أَكَلَ (ʔakala). The expected basic form would be *ekel or *ikel. The initial vowel was deleted by analogy with the forms of the 1st and 2nd persons, where it had been lost by regular reduction of unstressed vowels. The remaining vowel was then lengthened by analogy with a hollow root. L

Probably from Arabic قَاسِح (qāsiḥ, “hard”), in closely related Tunisian Arabic also كاسح (kāsiḥ). This adjective is used in Morocco in the collocation برد قاسح (bard qāsiḥ, “severe cold”). The sense “cold” could also derive from “hard” → “frozen” → “cold”, but this may be less likely given the extr
Inherited from Arabic كَيْفَ (kayfa). Compare Tunisian Arabic كِيف (kīf) and Moroccan Arabic كيف (kīf).
From Arabic كَلَبَ (kalaba, “to be rabid, mad, thirsty, greedy”).
Inherited from Arabic كُلْوِيّ (kulwiyy). By surface analysis, kilwa + -i.

parole.significato: to sweep (clean with a broom etc.)
to acquire; to obtain; to win (get through effort)
to smash, to shatter, to crush

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic كِتْبَة (kitba). Cognate with Tunisian Arabic كِتبَة (ketbə).

parole.significato: to uncover; to reveal; to disclose (make known something that was secret or dubious)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic إِكْلِيل الْجَبَل (ʔiklīl al-jabal).
Inherited from Arabic كَنِيسَة (kanīsa). Compare Tunisian Arabic كنيسية (knīsiyya), Moroccan Arabic كنيسية (knīsiyya), كنيسة (knīsa).

parole.significato: a ball of wool (other other thread-like material)

parole.testo: From Arabic كُلُّ شَيْء (kullu šayʔ, literally “every thing”). By surface analysis, kull + -x.

From Arabic كُلُّهُ (kulluhu, “all of it”). By surface analysis, kull + -u. The reason for the vowel change is that Arabic short -u- was predominantly shifted to -o-, but remained in closed syllables before the tone.
From kull + jum, from Arabic كُلَّ يَوْمٍ (kulla yawmin).
From Arabic كُلِّ مَكَان (kulli makān, “everywhere”, literally “in every place”). By surface analysis, kull + mkien.
From Arabic كُوز (kūz), from Middle Persian.

parole.significato: small balls of dough, used as a solid in soups
parole.testo: From Arabic كُسْكُس (kuskus), also كُسْكُسُو (kuskusū), from a Berber language.

parole.significato: Used—optionally—with a negated second-person imperfect verb to express the negated imperative.
parole.testo: From Arabic لَا (lā). Doublet of le (“no”).

parole.significato: to babble, chatter, talk much and idly
parole.testo: Onomatopoeic. The root may be inherited from dialectal Arabic; compare لبلب (lablab, “speaking fluently”) in Mid-Eastern dialects.
From Arabic الإبْرة (al-ʔibra), from إبْرة (ʔibra, “needle”) with fused definite article ال (al-).

From Arabic لَعّاب (laʕʕāb). Originally the noun was pronounced /laʕˈʕaːp/, while the verb was /ˈla.ʕap/. Both merged in the 19th century when għ was vowelised. The spelling lagħgħab, which is sometimes seen, is incorrect because għ can never be geminated in Maltese. However some speakers might stil

From a nasalised variant of Arabic الإجّاص (al-ʔijjāṣ), from إجّاص (ʔijjāṣ) with fused definite article اَل (al-). Compare Algerian Arabic لنجاص (lanjāṣ), Moroccan Arabic لنجاص (langāṣ) or نجاص (ngāṣ), and South Levantine Arabic إنجاص (injāṣ).

From Arabic لَقِيَ (laqiya, “to meet”). The unetymological final għ was triggered by the influence of q on the following vowel; compare baqa’. The etymological past participle milqi is preserved in the placename San Pawl Milqi (literally “St. Paul welcomed”).

From Arabic لَقَب (laqab) with irregular -m for -b; possibly by association with unrelated laqqam (“to graft”), as if the new name were “engrafted” onto the person. Compare Moroccan Arabic لقن (laqqan, “to call someone by their last name”).

Apparently from Arabic لَقَطَ (laqaṭa, “to pick up”). A development “pick up” → “grab” → “hit” might be conceivable, but probably influenced by such roots as لَكَأَ (lakaʔa), لَكَثَ (lakaṯa), لَكِدَ (lakida), لَكَزَ (lakaza), all meaning “to hit”. Compare also Yemeni Arabic لكد (lakad) in this sense
From Arabic لَقْلَقَ (laqlaqa, “to gabble, rattle”), perhaps denominal from لَقْلَق (laqlaq, “stork”).

Probably inherited from Arabic نارَنْج (nāranj, “bitter orange”), from Persian نارنگ (nârang). The -i- seems to be the result of imala and does not appear in any of the relevant Romance cognates. Since bitter oranges were cultivated in Sicily since the Arab reign, inheritance is also historically li

parole.significato: to reach, to manage to get to, to catch up with

parole.testo: From Arabic لَحْلَحَ (laḥlaḥa), which is attested with the opposite senses “remain fixed in a place” as well as “dislodge, move out of a place”.
Inherited from Arabic لَحْمِيّ (laḥmiyy). By surface analysis, laħam + -i.
From Arabic, related to لُبّ (lubb). Compare Moroccan Arabic بابة (bāba).
From Arabic اَلْبارِح (al-bāriḥ, “yesterday”). Compare Moroccan Arabic البارح (el-bāriḥ), Egyptian Arabic امبارح (imbāriḥ).

parole.significato: two days ago; the day before yesterday
parole.testo: Fossilised expression from Arabic الْبَارِحَةَ ٱلْأُولَى (al-bāriḥata l-ʔūlā).
From Arabic لَا (lā). Cognate with Hebrew לא (lō).

From Arabic لَقَفَ (laqafa, “to seize, catch quickly”) with metathesis. In older Maltese the verb also meant “to gasp for breath”, which explains the semantic development. A similar use apparently exists in some Maghrebi dialects.

parole.significato: night (evening or night spent at a particular activity)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic لَيْلِيّ (layliyy). By surface analysis, lejl + -i.

parole.significato: to, toward, towards (in the direction of, arriving at)
parole.testo: From Arabic إِلَى أَيْنَ (ʔilā ʔayna). By surface analysis, lil + *ejn. The personal forms are from Arabic إِلَى (ʔilā).
From a dialectal Arabic lallūš or lālūš, said to be of Berber origin.

From Arabic لَمَعَ (lamaʕa). The original inflection with a final għ is now less common (see above). Otherwise the root was reanalysed as ending in a semivowel. For this case, moreover, there exist two conjugations (one with -a- in all forms and one of the type of beda).
From Arabic يَمِين (yamīn) with assimilation /lj/ → /ll/ in the definite form الْيَمِين (al-yamīn), as also in llum and Lhudi.

parole.significato: to shine brightly, to gleam, glitter
parole.testo: From Arabic لَقَّ (laqqa, “to hit”). Compare Hijazi Arabic لق (lagg, “to shine”).

parole.significato: almond, almonds (several nuts; almond as a mass or species)
beard as an object of shaving; facial hair; stubbles

parole.testo: From Arabic أَلَحَّ (ʔalaḥḥa, “to insist, urge”, also of clouds “to rain continuously, to stay in one place”). The sense “to flash” from the persistent flashes of lightning during a thunderstorm.

parole.significato: drool, slobber (excessive saliva as e.g. in babies or old people)
Jew (an adherent of Judaism or a person who claims a tribal or ancestral connection to the Jewish people)
parole.testo: From Arabic يَهُودِيّ (yahūdiyy, “Jew, Jewish”). The definite form اَلْيَهُودِيّ (al-yahūdiyy) underwent assimilation -ly- → -ll- (compare llum from il-jum), whence a new basic form *lahūdī, *lhūdī by backformation.

From Arabic اَلَّذِي (allaḏī, relative pronoun). Compare common dialectal Arabic اللي (illi, lli). The use as a conjunction is widely found in Maghrebi Arabic, so there is no reason to consider it a Romance influence (as might otherwise be thought; compare Italian che, which is both a relative prono

parole.significato: beestings, colostrum (first milk after giving birth)
parole.testo: From Arabic لِبَأ (libaʔ, “beestings”). The vulgar sense after the thick consistency of such milk.

parole.significato: to clothe, dress (provide clothes for, put clothes on)
to shrink, draw back, cower fearfully (as in a corner)

parole.testo: Conflation of Arabic لُبَان (lubān) and لَهْبَان (lahbān).
From Arabic لِبْسة (libsa, “attire, choice of clothes”, in dialects also “garment, dress”).
From Arabic أَفْعَى (ʔafʕā, “viper”) with fused definite article. Compare Moroccan Arabic لفعة (lafʕa)

parole.significato: to fix the bait to a fishing rod
parole.testo: Probably from loqma (“bite, morsel”), from Arabic لُقْمة (luqma), with sporadic -k- for -q-. If so, a doublet of laqqam.

From Arabic لِ (li). The final -l may be due to backformation from the personal forms, themselves derived by reduplication. Compare Moroccan Arabic ليل (līl, “for”), North Levantine Arabic لإلي (laʔilli, “to me”), لإلك (laʔillak, “to you”), etc., reduplicated personal forms of ل (la). And compare a
From Arabic إِزَار (ʔizār) with fused definite article.
From Arabic اللَّيْلَةَ (al-laylata). By surface analysis, il- + lejla.
Contraction of il-jum, literally “the day”, from Arabic اَلْيَوْمَ (al-yawma).
From Arabic الأَسِير (al-ʔasīr), from أَسِير (ʔasīr) with fused definite article.

parole.significato: to meet (one another); to meet up
parole.testo: From Arabic اِلْتَقَى (iltaqā). For the addition of għ as a final root letter, compare the notes at baqa’.
From Arabic يَتِيم (yatīm) with the initial semivowel replaced with l under influence of the article, as also in Lhudi and illum.
From Arabic لَوْح (lawḥ, “board, plank, anything broad and flat”).
From the construct form of Arabic لِحْيَة (liḥya, “beard”). Doublet of leħja (“beard”), which becomes leħit-, lħit- before personal suffixes. The new noun lħit thence by backformation.

parole.significato: not; used to negate verbs and pronominal adverbs
maghrib, the sunset time of the Islamic prayer
Maltese (of, from or relating to Malta)
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic مالْطِيّ (mālṭiyy). By surface analysis, Malta + -i.

parole.significato: to criticise, put down, find fault with
parole.testo: Perhaps from the Arabic root ق ذ ر (q ḏ r) related to “being filthy, abominable, immoral”. Or perhaps from قَدَّرَ (qaddara) in the sense of “to imply, to call someone something”.

parole.significato: a holy place; a temple or place of worship
a place to sit; a spot or seat
pen, sty, stall (fenced area or compartment for animals)
parole.testo: From an alteration (*maqyal) of Arabic مَقِيل (maqīl, “resting place”).

parole.significato: a date-filled pastry fried in oil
parole.testo: From dialectal Arabic مَقْرُوط (maqrūṭ), from مَقْرُوض (maqrūḍ).
Inherited from Arabic مَارَ (māra, “to budge, to move forth, to fluctuate, to undergo commotion”) in form, influenced by Arabic مَرَّ (marra, “to pass”) in meaning.
From Arabic اِمْرَأة (imraʔa, “woman; wife”). Formally, a backformation from the latter’s definite form اَلْمَرْأة (al-marʔa) as in most modern Arabic dialects.

parole.significato: to cause someone to fall ill

parole.testo: From Arabic مَصْفَى (maṣfā, literally “place of purification”), a calque of Latin purgatorium, whence also the modern word. Arabic-speaking Catholics use مَطْهَر (maṭhar), an equivalent formation from a synonymous root.
Inherited from Arabic مِصْرِيّ (miṣriyy). By surface analysis, Masar + -i.

Univerbation of ma’ (“with”) + *ħaf (“fear”) + -i, literally “with fear”, *ħaf is possibly the verbal noun of hypothetical form I *ħaf from خَافَ (ḵāfa, “to fear”). Perhaps *ħaf has merged or superseded by ħaf (“to roam”), itself from a metathesis of Arabic حَفِيَ (ḥafiya, “to walk barefoot”). Compa
From Arabic مِنْ بَعْدِ (min baʕdi). Compare Tunisian Arabic مبعد (mbaʕd, “then”).
From Arabic مُبَاعَد (mubāʕad). Past participle of biegħed (“to remove”). Compare Moroccan Arabic مباعد (mbāʕad, mbāʕid).

parole.significato: to lay (something on a surface, especially one's hand)
a length, stretch (of time or space)
parole.testo: From Arabic مُدَّة (mudda, “while, length of time”).

From Arabic بَلَى (balā, “why, certainly!, yes, of course!”), in dialects also with prefixed m-. Compare Tunisian Arabic مِالَا (mēlə), South Levantine Arabic مبلا (mbala) and Gulf Arabic امبلة (ambala).

Derived from Arabic رَحَلَ (raḥala, “to saddle, to journey”), which in early Maltese was used of herdsmen and their animals; compare raħħal (“herdsman, stockbreeder”), from Arabic رَحّال (raḥḥāl, “traveller”). The underlying form is probably مَرْحَلة (marḥala) or *مِرْحَلة (*mirḥala), though the for

From Arabic مَوْت (mawt). The plural mwiet is originally that of the adjective mejjet (“dead”). It is still used as such in the set phrase qam minn bejn l-imwiet (“to rise from the dead”). The feminine gender probably through influence by Sicilian morti, Italian morte, both from Latin mors f; perhap
Possibly the passive participle of Arabic آوَى (ʔāwā).
Inherited from Arabic مَوْجِيّ (mawjiyy). By surface analysis, mewġ + -i.
From Arabic مُعَلِّم (muʕallim) and مُعَلَّم (muʕallam), participles of عَلَّمَ (ʕallama, “to teach”), whence Maltese għallem.
From Arabic مِغْرَفة (miḡrafa, “scoop, ladle”). Compare Tunisian Arabic مغرفة (mḡarfa, “spoon”), Moroccan Arabic مغرفة (mḡarfa, “ladle”).

parole.significato: not; negates nominal sentences, adjectives, adverbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic مَا هُوَ شَيْء (mā huwa šayʔ). By surface analysis, ma + hu + -x. Compare Tunisian Arabic مِاهُوش (mēhūš), مُوش (mūš) and Egyptian Arabic مُشّ (mušš).

Either inherited from rare Arabic مَبْغَضة (mabḡaḍa, “an object or cause of hatred”) or otherwise an independent formation from bagħad with the same measure. The underlying form is *mibgħda, where -e- was inserted to break up the inadmissible consonant cluster.

parole.significato: burial site; someone's grave; a place where one or more persons are buried

parole.testo: From Arabic مُذْنِب (muḏnib, “sinner, wrongdoer”). The plural midinbin is regular: The unstressed -e- is deleted, yielding *midnbin, where the -n- needs an epenthetic -i- because sonorants cannot stand between two other consonants. Compare the same in mislem, misilmin.

parole.significato: to speak intelligibly, to mumble one's words
to make someone roll on the ground
to run down, to criticize someone unfairly

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic مَأْكَلَة (maʔkala). Compare Tunisian Arabic ماكلة (mekla)، Libyan Arabic ماكلة (mākla)، Moroccan Arabic ماكلة (mākla).
From Arabic مَالِس (mālis), dialectal variant of مَلِس (malis). Compare Moroccan Arabic مالس (mālis).

From Arabic مِلْعَقة (milʕaqa, “spoon”, literally “licking tool”). A more etymological spelling would be milagħqa, because the underlying form is *milgħqa, where -a- was inserted to break up the inadmissible consonant cluster (as similarly in mibegħda). The spelling milgħaqa implies an Arabic *مِلْع

parole.significato: pupil (the hole in the middle of the iris of the eye)
parole.testo: Of onomatopoeic origin; possibly from dialectal Arabic. Compare dialectal Arabic مُمُّو (mummū, “pupil (of an eye)”), مُومُو (mūmū), مِمِّي (mimmī).
From Arabic مَن (man), dialectal Arabic مِين (mīn).
From Arabic مِنْ غَيْر (min ḡayr, “without”, literally “from other than”). By surface analysis, minn + għajr.
From a metathesis of dated milgħun (“cursed”), from Arabic مَلْعُون (malʕūn). Compare Moroccan Arabic منعول (manʕūl), Tunisian Arabic منعول (manʕūl) and Iraqi Arabic منعول (manʕūl).

From Arabic مِنْ بَيْنِ الْأَمْواتِ (min bayni al-ʔamwāti, “from the dead”), used with the same wording by Arabic-speaking Christians. It preserves an old broken plural of mejjet (“dead”), which has otherwise been regularized to mejtin in Maltese.
Inherited from Arabic مَسِيح (masīḥ). Doublet of messija.
Derived from silef (“to lend, loan”), from Arabic أَسْلَفَ (ʔaslafa). Thus unrelated to مَصْرِف (maṣrif), which means “bank” in contemporary Arabic (originally “stall of a moneychanger”).

From Arabic مُسْلِم (muslim, in dialects widely mislim). The word was inherited from Arabic as referring to a group of people with whom the Maltese remained in contact, while islam is a learned borrowing from Italian. Similarly, in other European languages, words for “Muslim” (like English Mussulman
Derived from staqsa, variant of saqsa (“to ask”), from Arabic اِسْتَقْصَى (istaqṣā, “to investigate, fathom, inquire”).
Inherited from Arabic مِئَتَيْنِ (miʔatayni). By surface analysis, mija + -ejn.
Puristic derivation from tar (“to fly”), from Arabic طارَ (ṭāra). Perhaps on the model of the analogous Arabic مَطار (maṭār).

parole.significato: winter residence, or any place where one passes the winter
an assembly, a gathered group of people

parole.testo: From Arabic مَجْنُون (majnūn, “mad, crazy”, literally “possessed by an evil spirit”).

parole.significato: a scale; a pair of scales

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic مِنْ أَيْنَ (min ʔayna). By surface analysis, minn + *ejn. Compare Tunisian Arabic منين (mnīn/mnāyn), Moroccan Arabic منين (mnīn), مناين (mnāyin).

From Arabic مَناخِير (manāḵīr), plural of مِنْخار (minḵār, “nostril”), whence Maltese minħar. Arabic dialects have widely lost the word أَنْف (ʔanf, “nose”) and replaced it with this word (either the plural as in Maltese, or the singular).

parole.significato: a unit of dry volume, that is officially 10.27 imperial cubic feet (290.9 L).

parole.testo: An extended form of Arabic مَعْذِرَة (maʕḏira).
From Arabic مُرّ (murr). Now usually declined like a Romance adjective with plural in -i.

According to Aquilina, from Arabic مُقَارِب (muqārib, “close to something”), as people that are naughty are generally annoying where to be so they would always be very close to you. Also possibly the active participle of a form III verb (*qareb) which no longer exists, if indeed it ever did, it prob

parole.significato: a handle to turn a wheel

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic مَصْلَحَة (maṣlaḥa). Compare Tunisian Arabic مصلحة (mṣalḥa, maṣlḥa, “broom”).

parole.significato: dark (not bright, especially through absence of light)
pocket knife, folding knife, jack-knife, switchblade
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic مُوسًى (mūsan). Compare Moroccan Arabic موس (mūs), Libyan Arabic موس (mūs).
Inherited from Arabic مِسْمَار (mismār). Compare Moroccan Arabic مسمار (musmār). Cognate with Sicilian musumarra~Musumarra.
Inherited from Arabic مُصْرَان (muṣrān). Compare Tunisian Arabic مصرانة (muṣrāna), Moroccan Arabic مصران (maṣrān, muṣrān), مصرانة (maṣrāna, muṣrāna).
From a dialectal Arabic مِشْعار (mišʕār), مُشْعار (mušʕār).
From Arabic مُحَلَّف (muḥallaf, “juror, one who has been sworn in”). The verb ħallef (“put under oath”) is now archaic. With respect to the underlying semantics a doublet of ġurat (“juror”).

parole.significato: First-person prefix in the imperfect conjugation
parole.testo: From Arabic نَ (na, first-person plural imperfect prefix). The use also for the first-person singular is found in Maghrebi Arabic dialects.
From Arabic نَعَى (naʕā, “to announce someone's death”). Compare the same semantic development in xeher.

parole.significato: to be sleepy; to doze off; to fall asleep inadvertently

parole.testo: Back-formation from nagħġa, from Arabic نَعْجة (naʕja, “ewe”).

parole.significato: to macerate, to ret, to soak
to weed, to remove the bad weeds from
a bit, trifle; a small thing or amount
parole.testo: From Arabic نَقْرة (naqra, “(not) anything”, in negation, literally “(not even) a snap of the fingers”).

parole.significato: a bell worn by animals (cows, goats, etc…)
to hunt for birds by trapping
stonemason (artisan who prepares and dresses stone)
side; direction (space in relation to some reference point, e.g. to the left or right of it)
bee, bees (several insects; the bee as a species)
to bray (make the sound of a donkey)
parole.testo: From Arabic نَهَقَ (nahaqa). Root-internal -h- does not normally become -ħ-. The development is probably expressive as it preceded the general loss of /h/. Vassalli already gives this word with /ħ/.
Inherited from Arabic نَحْلِيّ (naḥliyy). By surface analysis, naħal + -i.

parole.significato: to speak through one's nose, to twang
parole.testo: From Arabic نَغْنَغَ (naḡnaḡa, “to have an infected throat”). The final غ (ḡ) regularly became /ħ/ and this sound was then generalised throughout the root.

parole.significato: to seek access (to some group or field), especially through flattery and the like
parole.testo: The contemporary form is an analogical alteration of ndehes, but this is perhaps itself an alteration of ndess. Then further from Arabic اِنْدَسَّ (indassa, “to enter”, also “to visit in secret or in order to gossip”).
Back-formation from Arabic أَنْيَاب (ʔanyāb), plural of نَاب (nāb), compare Tunisian Arabic نيبة

parole.significato: to tease, to annoy, to spite

parole.testo: From Arabic نِمْس (nims), though the Maltese form is slightly irregular and points to an underlying *namas.

parole.significato: to strip, rid somebody of; to take (something) away from somebody
to burst into, to vent (an emotion or its expression)
parole.testo: From Arabic اِنْفَشَّ (infašša, “to deflate”), thus semantically like English vent or blow off steam.

parole.significato: daytime, day (time between dawn and nightfall)
to take root, to begin to grow, to form sprouts or buds

parole.testo: From Arabic نَبَشَ (nabaša) in the sense of “to elicit, draw forth”, hence “to provoke”.
