Inherited from Arabic نَدَى (nadā), feminised because of the final -a.

parole.significato: to initiate, launch (a program, project, etc.), to start something officially and publicly. Synonym: vara
to pierce; to penetrate; to puncture; to pass through

parole.testo: Intensive/frequentative of Arabic نَكَزَ (nakaza, “to drive, prod, spur”). Generalisation of /ɡ/ from assimilation to the following /z/ as in gideb, gidem.
From Arabic نَكْد (nakd) with generalisation of final devoicing throughout the root.

parole.significato: to cause sorrow; to sadden, grieve

parole.testo: From Arabic نِيل (nīl), from Middle Persian 𐭭𐭩𐭫 (nīl).

parole.significato: to procreate, to have children, offspring
parole.testo: Intensive and factitive of Arabic نَسَلَ (nasala).

parole.significato: to stink (have a strong bad smell)
to ooze, leak (flow out in small amounts)
parole.testo: Probably denominal from nixa (“leak water, leakage”), from Arabic نَشَع (našaʕ). This would explain the absence of the pharyngeal in the root, since word-final għ became weak early on. Alternatively intensive of the verb نَشَعَ (našaʕa).

parole.significato: -self; used with a pronominal suffix to form emphatic pronouns
parole.testo: From Arabic نَفْس (nafs, “self, soul, living being”), related with Maltese nifs (“breath”), from Arabic نَفَس (nafas). Regarding the initial gemination in some of the forms perhaps through the prepositional construction بِنَفْسِي (binafsī), بِنَفْسِكَ (binafsika), etc.

parole.significato: half (one of two parts, especially when equal)

parole.testo: From Arabic نِصْف اللَّيْل (niṣf al-layl, “midnight”). By surface analysis, nofs + il- + lejl.
From Arabic نِصْف النَّهَار (niṣf an-nahār, “midday; meridian”). By surface analysis, nofs (“mid, half”) + nhar (“day”). Sense 2 is a calque of Italian mezzogiorno.
From Arabic اِنْتَصَبَ (intaṣaba, “to stand, stand up”). Probably first broadened to “be in a place” regardless of posture (as also qagħad), and then narrowed again to sitting.
Derived from nieqes (“lacking”), naqas (“to decrease”), perhaps as an alteration of Arabic نُقْصان (nuqṣān, “lack”).
Inherited from Arabic نُخَالَة (nuḵāla). Compare Moroccan Arabic نخالة (nuḵḵāla).

parole.significato: areas; surroundings (of a city); parts (of a region)
parole.testo: With metathesis from Arabic نَوَاحِي (nawāḥī), plural of نَاحِيَة (nāḥiya), whence Maltese naħa.
From Arabic بَجْبَجَ (bajbaja), probably influenced by paċoċċ. Compare بَجْباج (bajbāj, “talking nonsense, garrulous, stupid”).
From Arabic بَجْباج (bajbāj, “talking nonsense, garrulous, stupid”).
From pit- + għada. The former is in all likelihood from Arabic بَعْدَ (baʕda, “after”), which has been lost in Maltese except in mbagħad. Compare Moroccan Arabic بعد غدا (baʕd ḡadda).
From Arabic بُشْط (bušṭ), from Classical Persian پُشْت (pušt).

parole.significato: The twenty-first letter of the Maltese alphabet, written in the Latin script.
to compare one thing to another (in order to contrast them and assess their respective similarities and differences)
to agree with; to assent to

parole.testo: From Arabic قَفَزَ (qafaza) with -b- from a development [fz] > [vz] > [bz] in some of the inflected forms (and in the related noun qabża). Compare the same development in beża’.

parole.significato: to sanctify; to hallow; to make holy
to close, shut (a door, window, or anything with a latch or lid)
to be, to stay (in a place)
state or position something is in
to put (animals) in a pen, sty

parole.testo: A suppletive formation: The third-person forms of the perfect are from Arabic قَالَ (qāla, “to say”); all other forms are from أَعَادَ (ʔaʕāda, “to repeat, say repeatedly”). The use of the latter verb in the imperfect tense is somewhat understandable, because one will more often mention the fact tha
From Maghrebi Arabic قَالَة (qāla). Related to Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian cala, and French cale.

From Arabic قَلَعَ (qalaʕa, “to pull out, rip off, uproot”). The sense “to vomit” perhaps reinforced by the fact that the verb (with its initial uvular and final pharyngeal) would have been somewhat onomatopoeic of retching; compare unrelated but phonetically similar Arabic قاءَ (qāʔa, “to vomit”).

From Arabic قَلْب (qalb). The feminine gender in Maltese is unusual since the Arabic etymon is masculine, its form is that of a masculine, and even the Romance equivalents (Sicilian cori, Italian cuore) are masculine. One might suspect influence by the semantically related ras (“head”) and ruħ (“sou

From qalb + -ieni, from Arabic قَلْب (qalb), perhaps after the expression قَوِيُّ القَلْبِ (qawiyyu l-qalbi, “courageous”, literally “strong of heart”). The same notion exists in many languages, compare German beherzt, English take heart, etc. Compare also the etymology of courage.

parole.significato: to turn over; turn upside down
a mould for baby cheese in the shape of a small hat or basket
parole.testo: From Arabic قالَب (qālab, “mould”), itself probably from Ancient Greek καλοπόδιον (kalopódion), the semantic relation with the above verb being coincidental.
From Arabic قِلَّوْط (qillawṭ). Cognate with Egyptian Arabic قلوط (ʔallūṭ, gallūṭ)

parole.significato: to get up; to stand up; to rise
a fathom (linear measure from the end of one arm extended horizontally to the end of the other) which was often used to…

parole.testo: From qamar (“moon”) + -i. Probably not inherited from equivalent Arabic قَمَرِيّ (qamariyy), but in the grammatical sense calqued on the Arabic.
From Arabic قُنْفُذ (qunfuḏ), through a common Maghrebi variant with a long ū for the second vowel; compare Tunisian Arabic قنفود (qanfūd), Moroccan Arabic قنفود (qanfūd).
From Arabic قِنَّب (qinnab), from a wanderwort related with Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis) as well as English hemp.
With dissimilation from Arabic قَلْقَلَ (qalqala, “to move, stir”).

parole.significato: a traditional unit of weight, still used e.g. in farming, equivalent to 100 ratal, that is officially 175 imperial poun…
parole.testo: From Arabic قِنْطار (qinṭār), from Classical Syriac ܩܢܛܝܢܪܐ (qanṭīnārā), from Ancient Greek κεντηνάριον (kentēnárion), from Latin centēnārium. Doublet of ċentinarju.
From dialectal Arabic, ultimately onomatopoeic. Compare Moroccan Arabic قاقى (qāqa) and North Levantine Arabic قاقى (ʔāʔa).

parole.significato: to pinch, to nip, to bite (insects)

parole.testo: From Arabic قَرِيب (qarīb). Doublet of the adjective qrib (“close, near”).
From Arabic قَرْمَشَ (qarmaša), an extended form of قَرَشَ (qaraša).

parole.significato: to confess (acknowledge one's sins in the sacrament of confession); (figurative) to confess; to admit wrongdoing

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic قَرَّابَة (qarrāba, “flask; carafe?”), derived from قِرْبَة (qirba) or قِرَاب (qirāb) better known as جِرَاب (jirāb).

If Arabic, perhaps from أَقْلَقَ (ʔaqlaqa), قَلَّقَ (qallaqa, “to upset, disconcert”). Or alternatively from قَرَّعَ (qarraʕa, “to blame, repoach; to win a bet”) with assimilation of the third radical to the first; compare also related قَرَعَ (qaraʕa, “to strike; to impugn; to reject a suitor in mar
From Arabic قَرْطَفَ (qarṭafa), extended form of قَرَّطَ (qarraṭa).

parole.significato: a paper wrapping for groceries, e.g. in the form of a cornet
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic قِرْطَاس (qirṭās). Doublet of karta (“paper in general, writing paper”).
From Arabic قَسْطَن (qasṭan), a variant of كَسْتَنَاء (kastanāʔ), from Ancient Greek κάστανα (kástana).

parole.significato: to kill, slaughter, murder (cause the death of a person or animal, in whatever way or circumstance)
a cut; an instance of cutting; the resulting slit

parole.testo: Probably singulative of Arabic قَثّ (qaṯṯ, “collecting, gathering”).

parole.significato: to let drip, to let dribble
hoof (tip of a toe of ungulates)

parole.testo: Univerbation of qaws Alla, literally “bow of God”, from Arabic قَوْس الله (qaws allāh, “bow of God”), pious alteration of قَوْس قُزَح (qaws quzaḥ), which was named after a pre-Islamic deity, but continues to be the predominant form in Arabic.

parole.significato: whore; slut; harlot (a prostitute or promiscuous woman)

parole.testo: From Arabic قَحْقَحَ (qaḥqaḥa), ultimately probably Onomatopoeic.
From the verb qażqaż (“to grunt”), from regional Arabic قَزْقَزَ (qazqaza), قَصْقَصَ (qaṣqaṣa, “to cry, call, make noise”).
Singularisation of Arabic أَقْداح (ʔaqdāḥ), plural of قَدَح (qadaḥ).
Derived from qaddis (“holy”) with the common measure for abstract nouns, perhaps as an alteration of Arabic قُدْسِيّة (qudsiyya), which would have yielded Maltese *qudsija or *qodsija.

parole.significato: A verbal particle indicating progressive verb tenses
parole.testo: From a contracted pronunciation of qiegħed, from Arabic قاعِد (qāʕid, “sitting”), used in a number of dialects (like Tunisian Arabic and Hijazi Arabic) to form progressive tenses, originally in the sense “he’s sitting there (talking, drinking, etc.)”. Unrelated to Arabic قَد (qad), a modal particle,
From Arabic قَضَى (qaḍā, “to perform”). Took over the sense of “serve” after خَدَمَ (ḵadama), Maltese ħadem, had itself come to mean “work”.

parole.significato: the olden days, old times, antiquity

parole.testo: From the merger of Arabic قَرِدَ (qarida) and Arabic قَرَضَ (qaraḍa).
Probably derived from Arabic قِرْق (qirq, “insignificant people”).
From Arabic قِبْلة (qibla, “direction of prayer towards Mekka”). The geographically peculiar use for “south” is also found in some dialects of Maghrebi Arabic.
From Arabic قاعِد (qāʕid), present participle of قَعَدَ (qaʕada, “to sit”), whence Maltese qagħad.

parole.significato: to put, to place, to lay
parole.testo: From Arabic قَعَّدَ (qaʕʕada), أَقْعَدَ (ʔaqʕada), factitive stems of the verb above.
From Arabic قَالَ (qāla, “to take a nap”).
From Arabic أَقَامَ (ʔaqāma, “to perform”, also a religious duty).

Probably from Arabic غِلّ (ḡill). Merger of غ [ɣ~ʁ] and ق [q] occurs regularly in some dialects of the Arabian penninsula and sometimes also in Sudan. While Maltese is generally not affected by this development, it was assisted here by the fact that the root ق ل ل (q l l) has some related senses. In

parole.significato: a jar or jug, usually earthen
parole.testo: From Arabic قُلَّة (qulla). Similarity with Italian olla (“earthen jar”) is coincidental.
Inherited from Arabic قُرْبَان (qurbān), borrowed from Aramaic קורבנא (qurbānā).
Of Arabic origin. Related to Andalusian Arabic "qurq" and "gurg" in rural Tunisian and Algerian Arabic.
Inherited from Arabic قُطْنِيّ (quṭniyy). By surface analysis, qoton + -i.
From Arabic قَرِيب (qarīb). Doublet of the noun qarib (“relative”).
Inherited from Arabic قَرَنْفُل (qaranful). Compare Sicilian Garòfalu.

Inherited from dialectal Arabic. The exactly corresponding form is found in Tunisian Arabic قرقّة (ʔruʔʔa, qroqqa, “brooding hen”), South Levantine Arabic قرقة (ʔruʔʔa, qruqqa, “brooding hen”). Compare also North Levantine Arabic قرقة (ʔirʔa, qirqa), كركة (krikka). Related to Arabic قَرَّقَ (qarraqa
From Arabic قُبَّيْط (qubbayṭ). Cognate with Sicilian cubbàita, cupeta.

parole.significato: a mass; a single celebration of the rite of Holy Mass
parole.testo: Singulative derivation from Arabic قُدّاس (quddās). One of the specifically Christian terms inherited from Arabic; compare isqof.
From Arabic قِرْدَان (qirdān), plural of قُراد (qurād).

From Arabic رَأَى (raʔā). An oft-cited archaism in Maltese as the verb has been displaced in most contemporary dialects (some preserved it though like Tunisian Arabic. View Tunisian Arabic رَا (ra)). The peculiar use of the imperative is similar to Maghrebi forms like راني (rāni) etc., which ultimat

From Arabic رابِع (rābiʕ). The ordinal numbers of 5, 7, 9 and 10 were originally distinguished from the attributive cardinal numbers by vowel length, e.g. ħames with [a] for “five” and [aː] for “fifth”. However, since numerals do not usually bear strong stress in the noun phrase, this distinction ul

parole.significato: to bring up, rear, raise, educate (a child)

parole.testo: From Arabic رَبْطة (rabṭa) and/or رابِطة (rābiṭa), which would probably have merged in Maltese.

parole.significato: any wheel that does not move forward, especially

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic رَغْوِيّ (raḡwiyy). By surface analysis, ragħwa + -i.

parole.significato: pledge, pawn, bail (money or item of value deposited as a security)

parole.testo: From Arabic رَاهِب (rāhib). One of the specifically Christian words inherited from Arabic, though in this case one that is widely known among Muslims (and also mentioned in the Quran).
Inherited from Arabic رَمْلِيّ (ramliyy). By surface analysis, ramel + -i.

parole.significato: Lent (Christian period of penitence and fasting before Easter)
parole.testo: From Arabic رَمَضَان (ramaḍān, “Ramadan”). The use of the word attests to the fact that—though Malta had been Christian before the Arab conquest—modern Maltese people mainly descend from converted Muslims. Arabic-speaking Christians otherwise use the terms اَلصَّوْمُ الْكَبِير (aṣ-ṣawmu l-kabīr, lit

From Arabic رَقَدَ (raqada, “to lie down, go to bed, sleep”). The normal Arabic word for “to sleep”, نَامَ (nāma), is entirely absent in contemporary Maltese, but compare obsolete newm (“drowsiness after a meal”).

From Arabic رَأْس (raʔs). The word is masculine in standard Arabic, but the feminine is found in some dialects, so there is no need to assume influence by Sicilian testa (though this is not ruled out).
From the Arabic root ر ص ص (r ṣ ṣ), which is related to “being compact, close together”.

Inherited from Arabic رَسُول (rasūl). Called an “arabism” by Falzon, but this may mean merely that the word was already highly archaic in the mid-19th century. At any rate it was inherited, not introduced later by Muslim captives, because old sources show that the place Għajn Rasul was always unders
Inherited from Arabic رَسُولِيّ (rasūliyy). By surface analysis, rasul + -i.

parole.significato: a traditional unit of weight, still used e.g. in household contexts, officially 1.75 imperial pounds (0.794 kg), now wi…
parole.testo: From Arabic رَطْل (raṭl), from Classical Syriac ܪܝܛܠܐ (rīṭlā), metathesis of ܠܝܛܪܐ (līṭrā), from Ancient Greek λῑ́τρᾱ (lī́trā).
Intensive derivation from raxx, from Arabic رَشَّ (rašša).

parole.significato: to marble, to cover with marble
to cheapen, to reduce the price

parole.testo: Factitive second stem of Arabic رَزَنَ (razana, “to be steady, firm, still”).
From Arabic رُدُوم (rudūm), plural of رَدْم (radm).

parole.significato: to spin cotton on a spindle
to blush (become red in the face)
to feed someone (especially on an empty stomach)
parole.testo: Denominal verb of riq (“saliva”), from Arabic رِيق (rīq). However, compare also North Levantine Arabic تروق (trawwaʔ, “to breakfast”) with the Maltese mediopassive trejjaq.

parole.significato: to lose weight, to become thin

parole.testo: From Arabic رِقّة (riqqa, “thinness, fineness, graciousness, diffidence”).
Conflation of Arabic لَصِقَ (laṣiqa, “to stick, adhere”) and Arabic رَسَعَ (rasaʕa).

parole.significato: a return, an instance of coming back or doing again
to be or feel very cold; to be freezing
parole.testo: From Arabic رَزَحَ (razaḥa, “to be exhausted, emaciated, to sink to the ground”).

parole.significato: the voiced velar or voiced uvular fricative /ɣ~ʁ/, an archaic phoneme in Maltese; see għ for more
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic غَيْن (ḡayn). The spelling ‹rgħ› is a merely linguistic convention, due to the use of [ʁ] for ‹r› in languages like French or German as well as in Maltese speakers with a rhotacism.
Intensive and factitive of Arabic رَعَدَ (raʕada).

parole.significato: to tread on, to trample down
to ride a horse, a vehicle

parole.testo: From Arabic رِزْق (rizq, “livelihood, sustenance; divine provision”), from Middle Persian 𐭫𐭥𐭰𐭩𐭪 (rōzīg, “daily bread, sustenance”). The new standard spelling with -s- is due to the fact that the noun has no root in Maltese, in which case words are now spelt phonetically rather than etymologically.
From Arabic رِيح (rīḥ). Originally a feminine, but masculine in Maltese (unlike related ruħ, which remained feminine).

From Arabic رُكْبَة (rukba). The modern Maltese form with metathesis, gemination and devoicing is a backformation from the plural (or original dual). From the expected *rokba, it would yield *rukbtejn, where the triple consonant cluster was simplified to *rkubtejn. Compare the same in mnifsejn (inst
Inherited from Arabic رَمَادِيّ (ramādiyy). By surface analysis, rmied + -i.
Inherited from Arabic رُكْن (rukn). Compare Moroccan Arabic ركنة (rukna).

parole.significato: pomegranate, pomegranates (several fruits; pomegranate as a mass, taste, species)

parole.testo: From Arabic رُوح (rūḥ). The expected plural is rwieħ with a post-consonantal variant irwieħ. The form erwieħ shows development of ir to er, as frequently in verbs, but otherwise not with epenthetic sounds. This unusual e- is therefore not felt as epenthetic anymore.

Probably from Arabic حَتَّى (ḥattā, “until; as far as; even”). The form, though without doubt unusual, might be explained from earlier *ħta by assimilation in fast speech. Compare Moroccan Arabic حتى (ḥta). Compare also Spanish hasta, which, if related, might point to the existence of an obsolete Ma
Inherited from Arabic أَصَابَ (ʔaṣāba). Compare Moroccan Arabic صاب (ṣāb).

parole.significato: to console (try to alleviate someone's sadness)
parole.testo: From Arabic صَبَّرَ (ṣabbara, “to make patient, summon to patience, console”).

From Arabic سَبَّتَ (sabbata), intensive of سَبَتَ (sabata, “to cut, smite, cast down”). The root partly overlaps with س ب ط (s b ṭ), which could explain the Maltese a-vocalism. It is likely that the verb was later associated with and influenced by the unrelated Sicilian sbattiri, Italian sbattere.
From Arabic سَدَّ (sadda, “to block”). Regarding the back vocalism in the root possibly merged with صَدَّ (ṣadda) with the similar sense “to hinder”.

Formally from Arabic صَدِيد (ṣadīd, “pus, ichor”), but the sense from صَدَأ (ṣadaʔ, “rust”). Compare Algerian Arabic صديد (ṣdīd, “rust”). Apart from their phonetic similarity, both Arabic words refer to impure substances forming on surfaces. Note also the rhyme with ħadid (“iron”).
From Arabic صَفاء (ṣafāʔ), feminised because of the final -a.

parole.significato: to be left; to come to be in some undesired state
parole.testo: From Arabic صَفَا (ṣafā, “to become pure, to remain after a process of purification”). The initial emphatic caused the addition of an unetymological final għ in some accents, whence the rarer variant sefa’ (compare the similar development in baqa’, laqa’, tema’).

parole.significato: a trip, voyage abroad, an instance of such travel

parole.testo: From Arabic صَعْتَر (ṣaʕtar), variant of زَعْتَر (zaʕtar, “thyme”). Compare Sicilian satra.

parole.significato: to wake (part of) the night (usually for work or religious devotions)
vigil (private or communal act of devotion at nighttime)
parole.testo: From Arabic سَهْرَة (sahra, “instance of waking the night”).

parole.significato: fishing (the act of catching fish; a fisherman's work)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic صَيْفِيّ (ṣayfiyy). By surface analysis, sajf + -i.
From chiefly dialectal Arabic سَكَّرَ (sakkara), a denominal verb derived from سُكَّار (sukkār).
Inherited from common Maghrebi Arabic سقصى (saqṣa), also سقسى (saqsa), an alteration of staqsa, from Arabic اِسْتَقْصَى (istaqṣā, “to investigate, fathom, inquire”).

parole.significato: to conceal, to cover up, to hide away

parole.testo: From Arabic صَوَّبَ (ṣawwaba, “to point, direct”, especially “to lower, direct downwards”, and hence also “empty a vessel”). Compare صابَ (ṣāba, “to come pouring down”, of rain).

parole.significato: to warm oneself, to get warm or hot

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic سُخْطة (suḵṭa). Compare Tunisian Arabic سخطة (saḵṭa, “curse, affliction”). See seħet for more.

parole.significato: to be safe, to be faultless
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic صَحَّ (ṣaḥḥa). Doublet of seħħ.
Inherited from Arabic سَبْعَةَ عَشَرَ (sabʕata ʕašara). By surface analysis, sebat + -ax. Compare Moroccan Arabic سبعتاش (sbaʕtāš), Egyptian Arabic سبعتاشر (sabaʕtāšar).

parole.significato: to become beautiful, to grow more beautiful
parole.testo: Ninth stem of sabiħ (“beautiful”), from Arabic صَبِيح (ṣabīḥ).
From Arabic سُبُول (subūl), originally plural of سَبَل (sabal), but also used interchangeably with it. Compare further سُنْبُل (sunbul).

parole.significato: to exceed; to be greater, better or more important than

parole.testo: Factitive of sabiħ (“beautiful”), from Arabic صَبِيح (ṣabīḥ). The verb is equivalent to Arabic صَبَّحَ (ṣabbaḥa), which at least in the standard language does not have this sense, however.

parole.significato: to realise, to cause to be effective or true, to affirm, strengthen
parole.testo: From Arabic صَدَّقَ (ṣaddaqa). As usual, the emphatic -ṣ- was dissimilated against the -q-.

parole.significato: share, portion (part someone has or receives, or that is due them)

parole.testo: From Arabic سائِر (sāʔir), active participle of سارَ (sāra). The verb was lost in Maltese as it became homophonous with sar (“to become”), from Arabic صارَ (ṣāra).

From Arabic صَلَّى (ṣallā, “to pray”, also “to pray for somebody, to bless”). Regarding the e-vocalism and the verbal noun tislija there may have been a merger with Arabic سَلَّى (sallā, “to amuse, entertain, comfort”). See the doublet salla for more.
Intensive of Arabic سَلَتَ (salata, “to cut off, extract”).
From a variant of Arabic سُلَّم (sullam). Cognate with Moroccan Arabic سلوم (sallūm).

parole.significato: trade, craft, sector of skilled work
parole.testo: From Arabic صَنْعة (ṣanʕa). The expected form would be *sangħa due to the originally emphatic ṣ, but this influence was levelled out or lost by dissimilation against the final għ (compare sejħa).

parole.significato: to chain; to enchain; to string together

parole.testo: From Arabic صَقْر (ṣaqr). The expected form would *saqar due to the originally emphatic ṣ, but this articulation was dissimilated against the q (as in several other words).
Inherited from dialectal Maghrebi Arabic. Compare Tunisian Arabic سردوك (sardūk) and Moroccan Arabic سردوك (sardūk).

parole.significato: an instance of stealing, a theft, robbery

parole.testo: Probably from Arabic سَرّاق (sarrāq), سَرّاقة (sarrāqa, “kind of small saw”). This may itself be a borrowing from a Romance derivative of Latin serra (compare Sicilian sirraccu, Catalan xerrac). However, the perfect phonetic identity between the Arabic and Maltese forms makes inheritance likely. If
From Arabic اِسْطَاعَ (isṭāʕa, “to be able”), a contraction of اِسْتَطَاعَ (istaṭāʕa, “to be able”), reanalyzed in Maltese as a Form 1 verb of a root s-t-għ.

parole.significato: a kind of veranda or terrace in a traditional Maltese house
parole.testo: From Arabic سَطْح (saṭḥ). Emphatic ṭ was assimilated to s and/or dissimilated against ḥ.

Verbal noun of seta’ (“can, be able”), itself from a reanalysis of Arabic اِسْتَطاعَ (istaṭāʕa). Semantically without doubt after Italian potere (“can, be able”, and as a noun “power, might, authority”), or rather its Sicilian equivalent putiri. Compare also Italian potenza, from Latin potentia. All

parole.significato: to cost, to be worth (to incur a charge, a price)
to mend, to solve (a problem, difficulty)
parole.testo: From Arabic سَوَّى (sawwā, “to make even, to smoothen”).

From Arabic سَخِطَ (saḵiṭa, “to be indignant, to resent”). Compare Tunisian Arabic سخطة (saḵṭa, “a curse”). The verb was used in Classical Arabic in phrases like اللهُ يَسْخَطُ لَكُم ذٰلِك (allāhu yasḵaṭu lakum ḏālik, literally “may God be indignant at you for that”). Accordingly, the subject must o
Inherited from Arabic صَحَّ (ṣaḥḥa). Doublet of saħħ.

parole.significato: a type of fried pastry, similar to Maghrebi sfanj.
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic إِسْفَنْج (ʔisfanj), borrowed from Ancient Greek σπόγγος (spóngos), borrowed from Pre-Greek.. Compare Sicilian sfincia.

parole.significato: Saturday, the cessation or last day of the week.

parole.testo: From Arabic سَيِّد (sayyid), widely also pronounced سِيد (sīd) in dialects.
Inherited from Arabic صَدْرِيَّة (ṣadriyya). By surface analysis, sider + -ija.

parole.significato: to journey, travel, make a trip of some distance (in the Maltese context generally implying going abroad)
a unit of dry volume, equivalent to 6 kejla, that is officially 111 imperial cubic inches (1.818 L).
parole.testo: From Arabic صَاع (ṣāʕ). As usual, the emphatic ṣ- was dissimilated against the final pharyngeal.
From Arabic سَأَلَ (saʔala, “to ask”). Compare Moroccan Arabic سال (sāl, “to be owed money”).
From Arabic أَسَاس (ʔasās). Compare Moroccan Arabic ساس (sās), Tunisian Arabic ساس (ses).

parole.significato: to follow persistently, to tail after
parole.testo: From Arabic سَاسَ (sāsa, “to lead, direct”) with semantic shift from leading to being led.
From Arabic سِكَّة (sikka). Doublet of zekka /zikka.
From Arabic سِكِّينَة (sikkīna), alternative form of سِكِّين (sikkīn).

parole.significato: to arrive after a long wait
to extract, draw out, pull out

parole.testo: From Arabic ثَلْج (ṯalj). Maltese s- (instead of expected t-) may be due to irregular assimilation of [θ] to the following alveolar [l]. The subsequent dissimilation š- → s- under the influence of following -j- would be less surprising (compare e.g. siġra).

parole.significato: to put on weight, to stout

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic سِمْسِم (simsim), borrowed from Aramaic שׁוּמְשֻׁומָא (šumššumā), borrowed from Akkadian 𒊭𒈦𒌑𒈬 (šamaššammum), from šaman + šammum.

parole.significato: to become hard (especially said of bread in an oven)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic سِنّ (sinn). The Arabic noun is feminine and was formally feminised in Maltese by adding -a; compare the same in widna (“ear”). Compare Moroccan Arabic سنة (sanna).
Inherited from Arabic سِلْسِلَة (silsila). Compare Moroccan Arabic سنسلة (sansla).
From Arabic سَرَجَ (saraja, “to shine”), which is denominal from سِراج (sirāj).
Inherited from Arabic سِتَّةَ عَشَرَ (sittata ʕašara). By surface analysis, sitt + -ax. Compare Moroccan Arabic ستاش (sittāš), Egyptian Arabic ستاشر (sittāšar).
From Arabic شَجَرَة (šajara) with dissimilation of š- against the following -j- (as in some Arabic dialects). Cognate with South Levantine Arabic سجرة (sajara) and North Levantine Arabic سجرة (sajra)
Inherited from Arabic سَمَاوِيّ (samāwiyy). By surface analysis, sema + -i.
From Arabic سُدّة (sudda, “door, threshold; seat, bed”, originally apparently “entrance area of a tent”).

parole.significato: sedge (any plant of the genus Carex)
there to be regret or sorrow; (in context) to regret; to be sorry

parole.testo: In all likelihood from Arabic أَسْفَراج (ʔasfarāj), from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos). While the Maltese -p- may be due to influence by cognate Sicilian spàraciu, the -ra- strongly points to inheritance.

parole.significato: to be plugged, to be stopped
to blush, to be ashamed, embarrassed, shy
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic اِسْتَحَى (istaḥā). Doublet of staħja.
Inherited from Arabic اِسْتَحْيَا (istaḥyā). Doublet of staħa.
From Arabic *اِسْتَأَنَّى (*istaʔannā), an alternative pan-dialectal form of اِسْتَأْنَى (istaʔnā).

parole.significato: to benefit from, to make use of, to exploit

parole.testo: From Arabic اِسْتَأْذَنَ (istaʔḏana, “to ask for permission to come in”). In Maltese, it has been transferred from the guest’s question to the host’s offer. Used the same way in Tunisian arabic.

parole.significato: to spend time; to socialise; to hang out

parole.testo: From a merger of Arabic اِسْتَمَلَّ (istamalla, “to regard as tedious”) and Arabic اِسْتَمَرَّ (istamarra, “to regard as bitter”). Phonetically both verbs still exist (as indicated above), but they are now merely variants of each other.

From Arabic اِسْتَراحَ (istarāḥa), a tenth stem from the root ر و ح (r w ḥ),hence related to riħ. In Maltese, a new root s-r-ħ was derived from this, perhaps to some degree by merger with Arabic س ر ح (s r ḥ), which is generally related to “moving”, but has some related senses like “grazing” and “be
From Arabic تَخَيَّلَ (taḵayyala, “to imagine”), altered as a tenth stem.

parole.significato: whistle (device used to make a whistling sound)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic سُلْطَانِيّ (sulṭāniyy). By surface analysis, sultan + -i.

parole.significato: common quails (Coturnix coturnix) (several birds; the quail as a species)

parole.testo: From a Maghrebi variant of Arabic سُخْن (suḵn). Compare Moroccan Arabic سخون (sḵūn).

parole.significato: Expresses the possessive or genitive: of, 's
parole.testo: From older Maltese bita, mita, from Arabic مَتَاع (matāʕ, “thing, possession”). Compare Tunisian Arabic متاع (mtēʕ), Moroccan Arabic تاع (tāʕ), نتاع (ntāʕ), North Levantine Arabic تاع (tāʕ), Egyptian Arabic بتاع (bitāʕ), all used as possessive markers.

parole.significato: to beat a drum, to drum
doctor (in the general sense, or a male doctor specifically)
sum of money to be paid coercively

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic طَائِفِيّ (ṭāʔifiyy). By surface analysis, tajfa + -i.

From Arabic طِين (ṭīn). Some older Gozitan dialects regularly diphthongised /iː/ and /uː/ in the vicinity of emphatic consonants. In tajn, this diphthongisation established itself more widely probably because it prevented homophony with tin (“figs”), from Arabic تِين (tīn).
From Arabic طَيْر (ṭayr). The singulative tajra may continue both طَيْرة (ṭayra) and طائِرة (ṭāʔira).

parole.significato: to become long, to become prolonged, to last
to ask for; to request; to beg
parole.testo: From Arabic طَلَبَ (ṭalaba, “to demand, ask, beg”). Though the Arabic verb can mean “to ask God in prayer”, the general sense “to pray” is not present. In Maltese, it is without doubt a semantic influence from Sicilian prigari (both “to ask” and “to pray”), from Latin precari.
Univerbation of tala (“come!”) + hawn (“here”). tala is from Arabic تَعَالَ (taʕāla, “come!”) which is ultimately of the same root as għoli.

From Arabic طَمَع (ṭamaʕ, “greed, wish”). The loss of the final għ is regular in this noun, but was generalised throughout the root (and is therefore reflected in the spelling). Compare, however, tema’.
From Arabic طَبْطَبَ (ṭabṭaba), eventually without doubt onomatopoetic (like the English equivalents and similar forms in several languages).

parole.significato: to weigh, be heavy on, burden

parole.testo: From Arabic طَقْطَقَ (ṭaqṭaqa), also تَقْتَقَ (taqtaqa), an onomatopoeic verb referring e.g. to the clacking of a horse's hooves and to stones tumbling down.
From Arabic دَرَج (daraj), plural of دَرَجة (daraja), whence the Maltese singulative. The t- is by dissimilation against the -ġ- (as in tiġieġ).

From Arabic تَرْبِية (tarbiya, literally “upbringing, rearing”), which is also used in the sense “foster child” by transfer from the action to its object. Compare Moroccan Arabic تربية (tarbya, “baby”).

parole.significato: tender; mellow; not tough or hard
parole.testo: From Arabic طَرِيّ (ṭariyy), reanalysed in the form of a present participle.
From Arabic تَرْس (tars), from Ancient Greek θῠρεός (thŭreós).
From Arabic طَحْنَة (ṭaḥna), instance noun of طَحْن (ṭaḥn).
Inherited from Arabic تَحْتَانِيّ (taḥtāniyy). By surface analysis, taħt + -ieni.

From Arabic طَهَّرَ (ṭahhara, “to circumcise”, literally “to purify”). The fortition of -h- to -ħ- happened early in this word; it is also reflected in the dictionary of Vassali, who otherwise always distinguishes these sounds.
Inherited from Arabic تَبَوَّعَ (tabawwaʕa). Compare Moroccan Arabic تبوع (tbawwaʕ, “to burp”).

parole.significato: one of two corresponding things, especially where one fits or shuts into the other
parole.testo: From Arabic طِبْق (ṭibq), طَبَق (ṭabaq), طَبَقة (ṭabaqa), or a merger of these.
From Arabic دَفَعَ (dafaʕa, “to push, thrust”) with regular assimilation of /df/ to [tf] in inflected forms and subsequent generalisation of the unvoiced consonant.
From Arabic دَفْعة (dafʕa, “push, thrust”) with /t/ after the underlying verb tefa’ (“to throw”), which see.
From Arabic تَكْتَكَ (taktaka), of onomatopoetic origin.

parole.significato: to ascend; to rise; to soar; to climb up (move to a higher position)
to leave; to depart; to go away
parole.testo: From Arabic طَلَقَ (ṭalaqa). The influence of the emphatic ṭ was dissimilated against the final uvular.
From Arabic أَطْعَمَ (ʔaṭʕama, “to feed”), either by simple metathesis or by association with طَمَع (ṭamaʕ, “greed, wish”), whence Maltese tama (“hope”).
Probably derived from Arabic تَنَفَّشَ (tanaffaša, “to ruffle, to flutter”), fifth stem of نَفَشَ (nafaša)
Inherited from dialectal Arabic, itself from Berber; compare Central Atlas Tamazight ⵜⴰⵏⴰⵖⵓⵜ (tanaɣut).
Inherited from dialectal Arabic, probably an extension of طَرَقَ (ṭaraqa). Compare Moroccan Arabic طرطق (ṭarṭaq).
From Arabic طَرْحة (ṭarḥa, literally “that which is thrown”), also used for different kinds of garments.
From Arabic ثُوم (ṯūm). The underlying form in Maltese as well as some Arabic dialects is ثَوْم (ṯawm).
From Arabic تَوْأَم (tawʔam). The expected form would be *tewwem. The form tewmi is either a backformation from the plural or derives from an adjective; compare Arabic تَوْأَمِيّ (tawʔamiyy).

parole.significato: a pile of straw, wheat on a threshing floor

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic تَفَوَّقَ (tafawwaqa). Compare Moroccan Arabic تفوق (tfawwaq).

parole.significato: any type of cereal (such as wheat, rice or oats)

parole.testo: Denominal from għażżien, from Arabic عَجْزان (ʕajzān).
From Arabic تَظْهِير (taẓhīr, “to be manifest”) or possibly local verbal noun formation of now obsolete *dehher.
Either an alteration of Arabic طَعِمَ (ṭaʕima, “to taste, eat”) or an independent derivation from togħma (“taste”), from related Arabic طَعْم (ṭaʕm), طُعْمة (ṭuʕma).
Back-formation from ttiekel, from Arabic اِتَّكَلَ (ittakala), reshaped to create a newly root t-k-l.

parole.significato: second (of a series or order, after first and before third)

parole.testo: From Arabic طاقة (ṭāqa, “window”), from طاق (ṭāq, “arch, doorway”), from Middle Persian tʾg (tāg, “arch”). The form tieqa instead of *taqa probably goes back to a variant *تاقة (*tāqa), in which the initial had been dissimilated against the q; compare dejjaq and others. Compare also Moroccan Arabic

From Arabic تَاج (tāj, “crown, diadem”). Semantically from a ceremonial headpiece worn on one's wedding day. Possibly the bride's chaplet (the symbol of her virginity), but more probably the wedding crowns of the Byzantine tradition, by which Malta was influenced in the Middle Ages.

From Arabic طِفْلة (ṭifla, “little girl”), feminine of طِفْل (ṭifl). Equivalent to tifel + -a. The plural bniet is from Arabic بَنات (banāt), thus originally plural of bint (“daughter”), but now not commonly used anymore to mean “female offspring” specifically, for which ulied bniet (literally “chil

Probably inherited from dialectal Arabic تَكّة (takka, “one, piece, morsel, bit, tad”), from Persian تکه (tekke), provided that the borrowing into Arabic happened early enough. Otherwise an independent onomatopoeia could not be ruled out; compare English tick (“checkmark; short moment”).
From Arabic. The root ك م ش (k m š) has several words to do with shrinking.
From Arabic أَتْلَفَ (ʔatlafa, “to ruin, spoil, waste”).

parole.significato: fig, figs: (several fruits; fig as a mass or taste)

parole.testo: Verbal noun of sella, which see for more. Perhaps in part directly from Arabic تَسْلِية (tasliya).

parole.significato: general term for a literary device where something is compared to something else: allegory, analogy, metaphor, parable
parole.testo: Derived from Arabic تَشْبِيه (tašbīh, “comparing, making similar”).
From Arabic دَجَاج (dajāj), with a change of initial by dissimilation.

parole.significato: to correspond, to write to each other

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ (ṯalāṯata ʕašara). By surface analysis, tlitt + -ax. Compare Moroccan Arabic تلتاش (tlattāš).

parole.significato: to quarrel, argue (have a verbal fight)

parole.testo: Probably derived from Arabic مُسْخَن (musḵan), مُسَخَّن (musaḵḵan, “heated”) in the sense “to get heated up”; or from a related word of the root. See Maltese sħun.
Inherited from Arabic ثَمَانِيَةَ عَشَرَ (ṯamāniyata ʕašara). By surface analysis, tmint + -ax. Compare Moroccan Arabic تمنتاش (tmantāš), Egyptian Arabic تمنتاشر (tamantāšar).
Inherited from Arabic اِثْنَا عَشَرَ (iṯnā ʕašara). By surface analysis, tn(ejn) + ax. Compare Moroccan Arabic تناش (tnāš).

parole.significato: to be workshy, to work little or reluctantly
parole.testo: Apparently from Arabic تَنَكَّرَ (tanakkara). The Maltese sense of workshyness (seen as a grave character flaw) could derive directly from the original meaning “to change to a dubious or negative state”. An alternative path might be “to disguise oneself” → “to feign, affect” → “to act unwillingly”.
From Arabic طَعْم (ṭaʕm, “taste”). Perhaps influenced formally by طُعْمة (ṭuʕma, “foodstuff, bite”), but an irregular development -agħ- → -ogħ- also occurs in some other Maltese words.

parole.significato: a unit of dry volume, equivalent to 10 siegħ, that is officially 0.6422 imperial cubic feet (18.18 L).

parole.testo: From Arabic ثَقالة (ṯaqāla, “heaviness”), compare English gravidity.

parole.significato: to cower, huddle (in a tight space)
parole.testo: Probably inherited from Arabic تَرَكَّنَ (tarakkana, “to be calm, firm, inaccessible”), but influenced by related rokna (“corner”).

parole.significato: street, road, way (any trail of some width for the movement of pedestrians or wheeled vehicles)
parole.testo: From Arabic طَرِيق (ṭarīq, “path, way, road”) and طَرِيقة (ṭarīqa).
Inherited from Arabic تُرُنْج (turunj, “citron”), from أُتْرُنْج (ʔutrunj), borrowed from Aramaic אַתְרוּגָּא (ʾaṯruggā, ʾaṯrungā).

From Arabic. The Maltese plural directly continues طُرْش (ṭurš), plural of أَطْرَش (ʔaṭraš). The singular might go back to an intensive/frequentative form *طَرُوش (*ṭarūš) or might be a backformation from truxija (“deafness”). Sense 2 is usually used for the geminated verbs, possibly called as such

parole.significato: to elbow (to push with the elbow)

parole.testo: A passive verb of an unattested *sief (akin to ttiekel, passive of kiel), ultimately from Arabic أَسِفَ (ʔasifa).
From Arabic اِتَّكَلَ (ittakala), reshaped to create a new root t-k-l.

parole.significato: apple, apples (several fruits; apple as a mass, taste, species)

parole.testo: From Arabic تُرْجُمان (turjumān). The -ċ- and the plural in -i point to influence by Italian turcimanno, but otherwise nothing speaks against inheritance.

parole.significato: to feel at ease in someone's company
to train, be trained (physically or in some skill)
parole.testo: From Arabic تَخَرَّجَ (taḵarraja, “to be educated”, modern “to complete a course, degree”).

parole.significato: and; used to connect words, phrases, etc.
parole.testo: From Arabic وَ (wa), from Proto-Semitic *wa. Cognate with Hebrew וְ־ (wə-).

parole.significato: a traditional unit of weight, still used e.g. in household contexts, equivalent to ¹⁄₃₀ of a ratal, that is officially…
parole.testo: From Arabic أُوقِيَّة (ʔūqiyya), from Classical Syriac ܐܘܢܩܝܐ (ʾūnqīyā), from Ancient Greek οὐγγία (oungía), from Latin ūncia.
From Arabic وَجِيع (wajīʕ, “painful”) and/or Arabic أَوْجاع (ʔawjāʕ), plural of وَجَع (wajaʕ, “pain”). Both forms would have merged phonetically in Maltese.
Inherited from chiefly dialectal Arabic وَنْوَن (wanwan), reduplication of وَنّ (wann), itself probably from classical أَنَّ (ʔanna).
Inherited from dialectal Arabic وَضَف (waḍaf), attested in Iberian Arabic and still in Maghrebi dialects.

From the Arabic root و ض ف (w ḍ f), variant of و ف ض (w f ḍ), which has to do with “accelerating”. The original sense is “shoot with a slingshot”, as still in the noun wadab (“slingshot”). This sense is attested for Iberian Arabic and still found in Maghrebi dialects. For the development f → b compa

parole.significato: to turn one's back on; to desert, shun, exclude (somebody)
parole.testo: From Arabic وَرَّبَ (warraba, “to make innuendos”). Compare also وارَبَ (wāraba, “to betray, to be two-faced against”). Apparently, the meanings “discard” and “leave” are generalisations from the original notion of “betray, turn one’s back on”.

parole.significato: to make arrive, to bring, lead

parole.testo: From Arabic وَحْد (waḥd). The forms from the stem weħid- before consonantal suffixes are influenced by related wieħed (“one”). The forms with waħed- appear to be compromise forms.
Inherited from Arabic وَحْدَانِيّ (waḥdāniyy). By surface analysis, wieħed + -ieni.
From Arabic وَحْوَحَ (waḥwaḥa). Possibly related to newwaħ.
From Arabic وَحْش (waḥš, “deserted, solitary; wild beast”). Compare also related وَحْشة (waḥša, “wildness, shyness, solitude, fear”) and وَحْشِيّ (waḥšiyy, “wild, uncivilised, cruel”).

parole.significato: a unit of surface area, equivalent to 4 tomna, that is officially 1.111 acres (4,496 m2).
to renounce, to give up, to surrender, to cede
to create, bring forth, cause to exist

parole.testo: From Arabic أَرَى (ʔarā), factitive IV. stem of رَأَى (raʔā), whence Maltese ra (“to see”). The Maltese perfect forms are backformations from the imperfect.

parole.significato: to bequeath; to devise; to leave (to an heir)

parole.testo: Formally from Arabic وَلْوَلَ (walwala, “to wail, lament”), itself probably from وَيْل (wayl, “woe”). The transitive use in Maltese would be a backformation from twerwer (“be scared”), from the fifth stem تَوَلْوَلَ (tawalwala), which in Arabic is used synonymously with the first-mentioned form.

Related to the verb werżaq (“to scream, shriek”), which has a plausible origin in a blend of werwer + obsolete żagħaq, themselves from Arabic وَلْوَلَ (walwala, “to wail”) + زَعَقَ (zaʕaqa, “to shout”). Werżieq would then be the agent noun of this verb (“screamer”). However, it is seems equally like

parole.significato: to be wide enough to have a capacity of; to be able to hold; to be able to accommodate
parole.testo: From Arabic وَسِعَ (wasiʕa, “to be wide, be able to hold”).

parole.significato: square (open space in a built-up area)
to widen, to broaden, to expand
to do, perform, accomplish, realise, put into practice
to hurt (cause someone physical or emotional pain)
to respect; to honour; to esteem appropriately

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic آتَى (ʔātā). Compare Moroccan Arabic واتى (wāta).
From Arabic جَاوَبَ (jāwaba, “to answer”), with metathesis.
Inherited from Arabic أَكَّال (ʔakkāl). Compare Moroccan Arabic وكال (wakkāl).

parole.significato: area of fields over a valley
inheritance; legacy (that which is bequeathed and inherited)
width, breadth (quality or degree of being wide, broad)
too, too much (more than is appropriate)
parole.testo: Possibly from Arabic وُسْع (wusʕ, “that of which one is capable, one's capacity, power”), with a rare shift from għ to q, which however could be accounted for in this phonetic position. Alternatively from وَسْق (wasq, “freight, load”); compare semantically English a load of (“much”).
Inherited from Arabic وَجْه (wajh). Compare North Levantine Arabic وج (wijj), وش (wišš), وتش (witš) and Egyptian Arabic وِشّ (wišš).

parole.significato: lizards (in practice especially geckos or lacertids)
a traditional unit of weight, still used e.g. in farming and household contexts, equivalent to 5 ratal, that is officia…

parole.testo: Contraction of earlier *iex (compare the reduplicated form xiex), from Arabic أَيّ شَيْء (ʔayy šayʔ, “what thing”), whence also Moroccan Arabic آش (āš), Hijazi Arabic إيش (ēš), Iraqi Arabic شِ (š).
From dialectal Arabic, from Persian شادی (šâdi, “monkey”). Compare Algerian Arabic شادي (šādi, “monkey”) and Gulf Arabic شاذي (šāḏi, “monkey”).
From the Arabic root ش ع ث (š ʕ ṯ), related to being “shaggy, disheveled, disordered”, especially of hair. Possibly referring to the hairs found on many kinds of caterpillars.
Inherited from Arabic شَهْر (šahr), from Proto-Semitic *śahr-.
Inherited from Arabic شَهْرِيّ (šahriyy). By surface analysis, xahar + -i.

parole.significato: synonym of Damaskin: Damascene (of, from or relating to Damascus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic شَامِيّ (šāmiyy). By surface analysis, Ix-Xam + -i.

Perhaps from a merger of Arabic شَنَّرَ (šannara) and شَذَّرَ (šaḏḏara), both roughly “to berate, blame, expose someone’s faults, make notorious, put to shame”, and thence generalised to “revealing, making known” in any context. In light of the frequent use in religious context (“spread the gospel”,

parole.significato: carpet bugle (Ajuga gen. et spp., or particularly Ajuga iva and Ajuga reptans)
to split, to make an incision
to make moist or wet; to moisten; to soak
beach; shore; bank; quay (any strip of land by a natural body of water)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic شَحْمَة (šaḥma). Doublet of xaħmet.

parole.significato: to be stingy, to become stingy.

parole.testo: Either derived directly from Arabic شَبِيه (šabīh, “similar”), or more probably with the measure of an abstract noun شَباهة (šabāha, “likeness, similarity”), which is uncommon in Arabic itself, but could easily be formed by analogy with such pairs as نَظِيف (naẓīf) ↔ نَظافة (naẓāfa).
From Arabic إِشْبِين (ʔišbīn), شَبِين (šabīn), from Classical Syriac ܫܰܘܫܒܺܝܢܳܐ (šawšəḇīnā). One of the specifically Christian words inherited from Arabic.

parole.significato: to be satiated, to be full, to have enough food
to resemble; to be similar to
male adolescent or young man; youth
female adolescent or young woman; girl (in this sense)
parole.testo: From Arabic شَابَّة (šābba), feminine of شابّ (šābb). By surface analysis, xebb + -a.

parole.significato: to satiate; to give somebody enough of (especially food)
to liken, to compare (to declare a similarity between to things, be it actual or figurative)

parole.testo: From Arabic شَبَه (šabah, “similarity”), perhaps merged with شِبْه (šibh, “something similar”).

parole.significato: to harness, saddle, or load (a pack animal)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic شَفَقِيّ (šafaqiyy). By surface analysis, xefaq + -i.

From Arabic شَعَلَ (šaʕala, “to light”). The same verb is used for “to turn on a machine” in several languages. In Maltese it may be a calque of Italian accendere, but compare also Moroccan Arabic شعل (šʕal), French allumer, Spanish encender (all “to light” and “to turn on”).

From Arabic شَهَرَ (šahara), أَشْهَرَ (ʔašhara, “to announce, spread, make public”). The contemporary sense developed in the context of death or specifically the announcement of a person’s passing by ritualised lamentation, which is found in some countries and formerly existed also in Malta.

parole.significato: desire (with a negative overtone and especially sexual); lust, lustfulness
to make someone old, or make them seem or feel old
to wave (sign by moving something back and forth, e.g. one's hand, a flag)
parole.testo: Intensive/frequentative of an obsolete *xar, *jxir, from Arabic أَشارَ (ʔašāra). Compare Moroccan Arabic شير (šayyar).
From Arabic شَيْئًا (šayʔan), indefinite accusative of شَيْء (šayʔ, “thing”). Cognate with Sfaxi Tunisian Arabic شَين (šayn)

Probably from the Arabic root ش و ر (š w r), which is related to “guiding, consulting” and “going, faring”. Perhaps verbal noun of the obsolete verb mentioned at xejjer and thus originally "indication".
From Arabic أَشْكَلَ (ʔaškala), شَكَّلَ (šakkala). Unrelated with English shackle, though speakers may now identify them with each other.
Inherited from dialectal Arabic. Compare North Levantine Arabic شلي (šili, “to speak ill of, to backbite”).

parole.significato: to chip, to hew off a piece from
parole.testo: Probably inherited from dialectal Arabic; compare North Levantine Arabic شلف (šalaf, “to throw”). The football sense is a calque of English chip.

Uncertain. Seemingly from Maghrebi Arabic شَلُوق (šalūq, “southeastern wind, scirocco”), whence also—perhaps through Romance influence—Maltese xlokk (“scirocco”). The Arabic word itself is said to be of Berber origin and this may explain the final -g (as there does not appear to be any case of Arabi

parole.significato: to sun, to dry in the sun

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic شَمْس (šams). Compare Moroccan Arabic شمش (šamš).
From xemx (“sun”) + -i. As such perhaps inherited from Arabic شَمْسِيّ (šamsiyy, “solar”), but in the grammatical sense a calque of the Arabic.

parole.significato: to hate, to bear ill-will towards someone

parole.testo: From Arabic شَنْق (šanq, “longing, yearning”). The senses of the root are generally related to binding and hanging, today chiefly as a form of execution. Perhaps the relevant sense can be derived thence from the idea that a person’s heart is bound and suffocating, or alternatively from accelerated b

parole.significato: to suit, to befit, to go along with
parole.testo: Perhaps from Arabic شَرَكَ (šaraka, “to share, partake, be a partner to”) with -q- for -k- as in several other words. Alternatively from شَرَقَ (šaraqa), أَشْرَقَ (ʔašraqa, “to shine”, also with beauty).
Inherited from Arabic شَوْكِيّ (šawkiyy). By surface analysis, xewk + -i.
Probably an extended form of Arabic شَلَحَ (šalaḥa). Compare North Levantine Arabic شولح (šawlaḥ, “to throw”)
Singulative derivation from Arabic شَوْق (šawq, “longing”), thus originally “a single instance or object of longing”.

Probably from or related with Arabic أَشْحَطَ (ʔašḥaṭa, “to remove, to put or send away”). Similar senses are found in Egyptian Arabic شحط (šaḥaṭ, “to put/throw dough in the oven”), North Levantine Arabic حشط (ḥašaṭ, “to throw”), Moroccan Arabic (Tangier) شعط (šʕaṭ, “to smash”).
From Arabic شُهُود (šuhūd), plural of شاهِد (šāhid), whence the alternative form above. The new plural xhieda on the model of such forms as bdiewa, Nsara.
From Arabic شَيْء (šayʔ, “thing, a thing, something”). Compare the same use as a determiner in Moroccan Arabic شي (ši) and North Levantine Arabic شي (ši).

parole.significato: span (the measure of the hand), officially 10 5⁄16 imperial inches or ~26.19 m.

parole.testo: From Arabic شِبِت, (šibit, also read as šibitt, šabat, “dill”).

From x’ + earlier *iex (“what”), of which latter x’ is itself a contraction, thus a reduplicative formation. *iex is from Arabic أَيُّ شَيْء (ʔayyu šayʔ, literally “what thing”), exactly equivalent to Moroccan Arabic آش (ʔāš). Also cognate with Hijazi Arabic إيش (ēš), where the contracted vowel is d
From Arabic شِيف (šīf, “prickles on the stems and branches of palm-trees”). The biological uses by analogy with the form of the beak and shell respectively.
Back-formation from the plural xwieni, from Arabic شَوَانٍ (šawānin), plural of شَوْنَة (šawna).

parole.significato: to survey, overlook, look (down) from a vantage point

parole.testo: From Arabic شِتَاء (šitāʔ, “winter, rainy season, rain”).
Inherited from Arabic شَيْطان (šayṭān). Compare Moroccan Arabic شيطان (šīṭān).
Inherited from Arabic شَتْوِيّ (šatwiyy). By surface analysis, xitwa + -i.
Ninth stem derived from xiħ, probably an alteration of Arabic شاخَ (šāḵa).
From Arabic شِكَارَة (šikāra). The Maltese -o- is unusual.
Probably from the dialectal Arabic verb for “to throw” mentioned at xellef.
From Arabic شَلُوق (šalūq), شَلُوك (šalūk, “southeastern wind”), probably acquired through Italo-Romance, see Italian scirocco. A doublet may be at hand in xellug (“left”), which see.
From Arabic شَنَاعَة (šanāʕa, “repulsiveness, abomination”), probably referring to the scandalous subject matter, but perhaps also because gossip is itself repulsive.

Among the variants attested in early sources are xilxi(n) and ixili(li)x. Hence probably from underlying xejn lil xejn or xi lil xi, equivalent to Arabic شَيْءٌ لِشَيْءٍ (šayʔun lišayʔin, “one thing to another”, literally “a thing to a thing”).

parole.significato: the hair of the head, especially when long

parole.testo: Probably an alteration of żekżek (“to peep, chirp”), from Arabic زَقْزَقَ (zaqzaqa). The change from [z] to the harsher [t͡s] perhaps onomatopoetic for muffled, aggressive speech.
Inherited from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar). The expected form would be *sokkor (or *sokkar). The onset z- is due to influence by Sicilian zuccru, itself borrowed from the Arabic.

Inherited from Maghrebi Arabic اِسْفَنَّرِيّة (isfannariyya), from Arabic إِسْفَنَارِيَّة (ʔisfanāriyya), from Ancient Greek σταφυλίνη ἀγρία (staphulínē agría, “wild carrot”). Cognate to Libyan Arabic سفنّاريّة (sfənnāriyya) and several Iberian languages; see Spanish zanahoria.
From dialectal Arabic شَعْلَق (šaʕlaq) likely from Arabic سلق.
From Arabic شَرَّطَ (šarraṭa) with irregular ċ- for x-.
From Arabic, related to Arabic جَصَّصَ (jaṣṣaṣa).

parole.significato: to deny, disclaim, refuse, renounce, repudiate (something)
parole.testo: From Arabic جَحَدَ (jaḥada), with generalisation of the regular assimilation [d͡ʒħ] → [t͡ʃħ].

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Unclear; Possibly; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly related to Egyptian Arabic شبورة (šabbūra), also شابورة (šābūra, “mist”). Since sonorants are often used to extend roots, the final r need not be original. In that case, it may pertain to Arabic شُؤْبُوب (šuʔbūb, “shower of hail or rain, vehemence of heat”, and in one old source

From common dialectal Arabic جَاب (jāb), from a univerbation of جاءَ بِ (jāʔa bi-, literally “to come with”). By surface analysis, ġie + b’. The vowel -a- is irregular; the expected form is the less common variant ġieb.
From Arabic جَرَّة (jarra). Cognate with Sicilian giarra.

parole.significato: to demolish, to cause to collapse
jewellery, jewels or precious stones and ornaments
to barely manage; to perform an action with difficulty; to scrape through
to renew, to make (like) new, to refresh, revive
to leather, to cover in leather
hazelnut, hazelnuts (several nuts; hazelnut as a mass or species)
to emit soot, to be sooty
parole.testo: From Arabic جَمَّدَ (jammada). The contemporary senses follow the semantic development of ġmied (“soot”).

parole.significato: paradise (idealistic abode in this world, e.g. that of Adam and Eve)
parole.testo: From Arabic جَنّة (janna, “garden; paradise”), from whose plural also ġnien (“garden”).

parole.significato: to wound; to injure seriously and bloodily
a wicker basket, typically with a handle
parole.testo: From Arabic جَوْلَق (jawlaq, “kind of sack or bag”), alteration of جُوَالَق (juwālaq), from Middle Persian [Term?] (/⁠guwālak⁠/).

Back-formation from the plural ġwienaħ, itself from Arabic جَوَانِح (jawāniḥ), as if from a four-radical *جَوْنَح (*jawnaḥ), but actually plural of جَانِح (jāniḥ, “side, wing”). Compare also جَنَاح (janāḥ).
Inherited from Arabic جَوَّانِيّ (jawwāniyy). By surface analysis, ġewwa (“inside”) + -ieni.
From Arabic جَزَى (jazā). Doublet of iżża (only with ħajr, "to give thanks").
Inherited from Arabic جِهَاز (jihāz). Compare to Tunisian Arabic جْهاز (“bride's wardrobe”).
From Arabic جَذَبَ (jaḏaba) with metathesis. Compare Tunisian Arabic جبِد (jbed) and Moroccan Arabic جبد (jbad).
Inherited from Arabic جِبْسِيّ (jibsiyy). By surface analysis, ġibs + -i.
From Arabic جَيِّد (jayyid, “good”). Compare the older form ġajjid, as seen in older Maltese texts. As a possible semantic influence, compare also Italian beni (“goods, means, riches”).

From Arabic جَاءَ (jāʔa, “to come”). As in some Arabic dialects, a suppletive form is usually used for the imperative. Maltese ejja, ejjew seem to be from the interjection هَيَّا (hayyā, “come!, come on!, let’s go!”). Since Maltese h would have left no phonetic trace in this position, the lack of it
From the intensive form of Arabic جَعَلَ (jaʕala).
From Arabic جَاه (jāh). Compare Moroccan Arabic جاه (jāh).

parole.significato: week (unit of time lasting seven days)

parole.testo: From Arabic جِلاد (jilād, “sword fight”), جِدال (jidāl, “fight, quarrel”).
From Arabic جَمَاد (jamād, “solid matter, dry and barren soil”).
From Arabic جِنَان (jinān), plural of جَنَّة (janna). Compare Tunisian Arabic جنان (“garden”).
From Arabic جُبَّة (jubba), or via Italian giubba and/or Sicilian giubba.
From Arabic جُمَانَة (jumāna), singulative of جُمَان (jumān).
From Arabic جُرْذَان (jurḏān), plural of جُرَذ (juraḏ, “rat”).
From Arabic جُوَيِّد (juwayyid), diminutive of جَيِّد (jayyid).
Formally from Arabic تَجالَدَ (tajālada, “to fight each other by sword”). Compare also تَجادَلَ (tajādala, “to fight, quarrel”). The two roots may be old variants of each other.

parole.significato: The eleventh letter of the Maltese alphabet, called ħe and written in the Latin script.
parole.testo: The letter mainly continues Arabic ح (ḥ) and Arabic خ (ḵ). These two phonemes were merged into /ħ/ around Valletta since at least the 18th century, but continued to be distinguished as /ħ/ and /x~χ/ elsewhere. By the later 19th century, however, this merger had established itself throughout the lang

From Arabic أَخَذَ (ʔaḵaḏa). Disregarding the different vowel colour (triggered by the ħ-), the vocalic development was exactly the same as in kiel (“to eat”), which see. The paradigm was further complicated by an unusual loss of -d in all word-final positions (except for the participle); this is al
Agent noun of ħabar, from Arabic أَخْبَرَ (ʔaḵbara).

parole.significato: to knock, to strike, to beat

parole.testo: Belonging to a four-consonantal root of uncertain origin. Most probably an extension of one of the following Arabic roots (or a merger of them): * Joseph Aquilina linked it with ح ب ك (ḥ b k); compare حَبَكَ (ḥabaka, “to tighten, make firm, do properly”). * Reinhart Dozy linked it with ح ر ك (ḥ r k)
Agent noun of archaic ħadar (“to be present”), from Arabic حَضَرَ (ḥaḍara).

parole.significato: to make something green (e.g. an area by planting trees)
to roam, to wander, to shuffle along
parole.testo: Perhaps from a metathesis of Arabic حَفِيَ (ḥafiya, “to walk barefoot; to abrade one’s feet by lengthy walking”). Joseph Aquilina mentions that ħafi (“barefoot”) was also used in the sense of “roamer”, thus preserving here the original participle form. There may have been a merger with حافَ (ḥāfa),
From Arabic غَفَرَ (ḡafara) with irregular devoicing of the onset as also in ħasel (“to wash”), from assimilation to the following -f- in conjugated forms.
Intensive second stem replacing ħafer, from Arabic حَفَرَ (ḥafara), in order to avoid the homophony with ħafer (“to forgive”), from Arabic غَفَرَ (ḡafara).

From Arabic حَفْنة (ḥafna, “a handful”). The word refers to a small amount in Arabic, but developed the sense “much, many” over time; compare English pretty, rather (both “somewhat”, but also “very”), or quite a few.
From Arabic خَافُور (ḵāfūr). The similarity with German Hafer etc. is coincidental.

Describing conservative accents of the early 19th century, Vassalli distinguished between two verbs, one with /ħ/ meaning “to allure” and one with /χ/ meaning “to let someone choose”. The contemporary ħajjar thus continues Arabic حَيَّرَ (ḥayyara, “to confuse, abash”). The semantic connection may be
From Arabic خَيْر (ḵayr, “good, goodness”). For the sense compare the phrase جَزاكَ اللهُ خَيْرَا (jazāka llāhu ḵayrā, “thank you!”, literally “may God give you good reward!”).
From Arabic حَيْرَة (ḥayra, “confusion, bafflement”). For the sense, compare the verb ħajjar.

parole.significato: thread, threads (a ball, web, or indefinite number)
parole.testo: From Arabic خَيْط (ḵayṭ), reinterpreted as a collective.

parole.significato: to rule, especially by force; to subdue

parole.testo: From Arabic خَال (ḵāl, “beauty spot”). Compare Moroccan Arabic خالة (ḵāla, “beauty spot”)

parole.significato: to swear, to take an oath
to loosen, to untie, to dissolve
to leave (someone or something in a place)

parole.testo: From Arabic حَلْق (ḥalq, “throat”). Cognate with Gulf Arabic حلج (ḥalj, “mouth”).

parole.significato: silt, sludge, ooze (fine mud as found especially near the seashore)
parole.testo: From Arabic حَمَأ (ḥamaʔ). The word predominantly keeps its masculine gender in Maltese, but may also be feminised on account of the final -a.
Probably from ħambaq (“to argue loudly”) with loss of the final radical. The verb is inherited from dialectal Arabic; compare Najdi Arabic خنبقة (ḵanbaga, “something messy, unorderly”).

Inherited from dialectal Arabic. Compare Najdi Arabic خنبقة (ḵanbaga, “something messy, unorderly”) and Hijazi Arabic خنبقة (ḵanbaga). However, could also possibly be related to (or otherwise influenced by) the Arabic root ح م ق (ḥ m q) related to foolishness and furiousness.

parole.significato: to ruminate, to think excessively about, to be unable to forget
parole.testo: Probably from Arabic خَمَّنَ (ḵammana); compare Moroccan Arabic خمم (ḵammam, “to think”), Tunisian Arabic خمّم (ḵammem, “to think”). Alternatively a derivation from حَمّ (ḥamm, “to heat”), as in “get heated up” (compare tmasħan), or from هَمّ (hamm, “to worry”).

parole.significato: earth; soil (organic material which covers the land)
parole.testo: Pertaining to aħmar (“red”). Probably an extended form of Arabic حُمَر (ḥumar), حُمْرة (ḥumra), which are also used of certain kinds of soil. Compare Moroccan Arabic حمري (ḥamri, “red earth”).

parole.significato: hamza (Arabic sign representing a glottal stop)

parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic حَنَش (ḥanaš), from Proto-Semitic *naḥaš-.
Inherited from Arabic خُنْفُس (ḵunfus). Compare Moroccan Arabic خنفوس (ḵanfūs).
Apparently an alteration of Arabic حَنُون (ḥanūn) after the common adjective measure C-(a)-C-i-C. Compare Moroccan Arabic حنين (ḥnīn).
From Arabic حَانُوت (ḥānūt), cognate with Aramaic חָנוּתָא/ܚܳܢܽܘܬܴܐ (ḥānūṯā).

According to Vassalli's dictionary with an original initial ح (ḥ). Hence probably related with Arabic حَشَرَ (ḥašara, “to destroy; to sharpen a knife”, among other senses). Compare also حَنَشَ (ḥanaša, “to hunt, catch”, and of a venomous animal “to bite”). And compare the semantic relation between ح

parole.significato: to escape, to run away; to avoid
parole.testo: From Arabic هَرَبَ (haraba) with the h- irregularly strengthened to ħ-, possibly due to the presence of the hard -b.

parole.significato: to disrupt, devastate, to cause chaos and disarray
parole.testo: From Arabic خَرْبَطَ (ḵarbaṭa). Possibly related to ħarbex.
From Arabic خَرْبَشَ (ḵarbaša, “to scratch”). The sense “scribble” is also attested. Probably an extended form of خَرَبَ (ḵaraba, “to ruin”).

From Arabic حارَسَ (ḥārasa), rare variant of حَرَسَ (ḥarasa, “to guard, watch over, protect”), or an independent alteration of the latter. The semantic development under influence of Sicilian guardari, from Frankish *wardōn, perhaps additionally also of ussirvari, from Latin observare.

In the present form it should be from Arabic حارِس (ḥāris, “guard, guardian”), active participle of حَرَسَ (ḥarasa) above; quite plausibly through the idea that ghosts watch over, or haunt, certain localities. The unusual plural iħirsa (from underlying *iħrsa as in iġsma) might then be explained as

parole.significato: to go out, to come out, to exit
ears (fruiting body of a grain plant)
to tell fibs, make up stories
carob (fruit and tree of Ceratonia siliqua L.)

parole.testo: From Arabic غَسَلَ (ḡasala) with irregular devoicing of the onset as also in ħafer (“to forgive”), from assimilation to the following -s- in conjugated forms.

parole.significato: shame, pity; as in “it’s a shame/pity that...”

parole.testo: From Arabic حَسَّ (ḥassa), أَحَسَّ (ʔaḥassa). The reflexive construction with pronominal suffixes is slightly unusual but not without precedent in Classical Arabic; compare أَظُنُّنِي (ʔaẓunnunī, “I consider myself”). In Maltese ħass, it probably mirrors the construction of Sicilian si sèntiri, from

parole.significato: to cause to rot, make rotten
to be to blame, at fault, guilty
to seize, to grasp, to snatch
to elect; to choose by vote
parole.testo: From Arabic اِخْتارَ (iḵtāra), an eighth stem from the root خ ي ر (ḵ y r). Reinterpreted in Maltese as a ninth stem from a root ħ-t-r (older Maltese ħtar), then reconstrued as a first stem. Doublet of ħajjar.

From Arabic. At least two roots are comparable and the Maltese is perhaps from a merger of them: 1.) حَظِر (ḥaẓir, “picket, cane for a fence”), حِظار (ḥiẓār, “fence, enclosure”); 2.) خِطْر (ḵiṭr, “branch of a tree”), خَطّار (ḵaṭṭār, “camel’s tail, pendulum, quivering spear”). If the original meaning

parole.significato: to unload, offload, remove from a vehicle or container (and store somewhere)
parole.testo: Inherited from Arabic حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, “to put down”).

parole.significato: peach, peaches (several fruits; peach as a mass, taste, species)

parole.testo: Possibly an extended form of Arabic خَشُنَ (ḵašuna, “to be rough”) where n -> l.

From Arabic حاجة (ḥāja, “need, necessity”). The sense “thing” is present in many Arabic dialects, including all African ones. It originated as a generalization of “necessity” in the sense of “thing[s] needed for some purpose”. Some of those dialects make a distinction in the plural between حاجَات (ḥ
From Arabic حَجَر (ḥajar, “stone”), which was reinterpreted as collective. Compare Moroccan Arabic حجر (ḥjar, “stones”), حجرة (ḥajra, “a stone”).
Inherited from Arabic حَجَرِيّ (ḥajariyy). By surface analysis, ħaġar + -i.
From Arabic حُزْن (ḥuzn). For the semantics compare ħażin.

parole.significato: to mourn, to put on mourning

parole.testo: From Arabic حَزِين (ḥazīn, “sad”). The semantic development was probably influenced by Sicilian tristu (“evil”) and tristi (“sad”), a doublet pair from Latin tristis (“sad”). Generally such a development is understandable from contexts like “sad news” and “bad news”, where they are more or less syno
Inherited from Arabic أَحَدَ عَشَرَ (ʔaḥada ʕašara). By surface analysis, (wie)ħed + -ax. Compare Moroccan Arabic حداش (ḥdāš).
Inherited from Arabic حِذَاءَ (ḥiḏāʔa). Compare Moroccan Arabic حدا (ḥdā), حداين (ḥdāyin, “near”).

parole.significato: to attack, to assault; to rush at
to give life to, to revive, to vivify

parole.testo: From Arabic هَيَّأَ (hayyaʔa, “to prepare, arrange”) with fortition of h- to ħ- as in some other stems such as in ħarab.
From Arabic هَيْم (haym), verbal noun of هَامَ (hāma, “to be madly in love”).
From Arabic أَخْلَى (ʔaḵlā, “to make void, vacant, deserted”).

parole.significato: to become sweet; (figuratively) to become kind

parole.testo: From Arabic خَلَصَ (ḵalaṣa, “to get rid”). Also adopted the transitive sense of Arabic خَلَّصَ (ḵallaṣa).
Maltese derivation from ħieles (“free”), from Arabic خالِص (ḵāliṣ); replaced ħlas (now only “payment”).

parole.significato: to have mercy; to be merciful

parole.testo: From Arabic حِنّاء (ḥinnāʔ). Probably not inherited, but borrowed through English henna, Italian henna.

parole.significato: to blaze, to emit a flame
parole.testo: From Arabic هَجَّجَ (hajjaja, “to fan flames, to fire up”) with irregular fortition of h to ħ as also, for example, in ħarab and ħejja. Compare related Maltese ħuġġieġa (“bonfire”).

parole.significato: a way, the ability to do something
parole.testo: From Arabic حِيلَة (ḥīla, “ruse, maneuver”). The phrase لَا حِيلةَ لَهُ (lā ḥīlata lahu, literally “he has no maneuver”) is used with a similar meaning as in Maltese; and compare حَيْل (ḥayl, “power”).

From Arabic غِلاف (ḡilāf). The devoiced onset is due to a merger of the Arabic roots غ ل ف (ḡ l f) and خ ل ف (ḵ l f) in Maltese. Vassalli gives the verb ħellef, ħallef (“to peel, husk”) with both /ɣ/ and /x/, and does the same, vice versa, with ħlief (“except”). The semantic interface between them w
From Arabic خَلِيقَة (ḵalīqa, “something created, creature, creation”).

From ħmar (“ass, donkey; jackass”) + -ija, equivalent to Arabic حِمارِيّة (ḥimāriyya), which is occasionally found in the same sense. Uncertain whether inherited or independent, though the -e- (vis-à-vis the -a- in ħmar) shows that the formation goes back at least to a time when imala was still acti
From Arabic أَخْماج (ʔaḵmāj), plural of خَمَج (ḵamaj, “putrefication, decay”), from خَمَجَ (ḵamaja, “to rot, putrefy”). Compare Tunisian Arabic خْماج (“dirt”).

Inherited from Arabic خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ (ḵamsata ʕašara). By surface analysis, ħamest + -ax. Compare Moroccan Arabic خمستاش (ḵmastāš), Tunisian Arabic خمستاش (ḵmastāš), Gulf Arabic خمستعش (ḵəmistəʕəš), Egyptian Arabic خمستاشر (ḵamastāšar).

parole.significato: dreams; dream as a state; dreaming

parole.testo: Verbal noun of ħalaq (“to create”). Compare Arabic خَلْق (ḵalq), of which it is perhaps an extended form.

parole.significato: to strangle, to throttle, to choke

parole.testo: From Arabic حِرْمة (ḥirma, “sexual desire”, especially of female animals “heat, rut”).

parole.significato: to shed leaves; to moult; to lose hair

parole.testo: From Arabic حَرِمَ (ḥarima, “to be in heat”), related to its root probably through the idea of being deprived and therefore keen.

parole.significato: the wall or rim around a well
parole.testo: From Arabic خُرْزة (ḵurza, “seam, stitch, round hole”).

parole.significato: matchmaking (the work of a matchmaker; the process of arranging a marriage)
harvest (act of reaping; that which has been reaped)

parole.testo: From Arabic اِحْتَاجَ (iḥtāja, “to need”). The impersonal use seems to mirror that of Italian bisognare, but the Arabic passive يُحْتاجُ أَن (yuḥtāju ʔan) is also used in this way, so the Romance influence is not certain.
From Arabic أَخُو (ʔaḵū), construct form of أَخ (ʔaḵ, “brother”).

parole.significato: fish (several fish; fish as a mass)
parole.testo: From Arabic حُوت (ḥūt), which was reinterpreted as collective and provided with the singulative -a.
Singularisation of Arabic خُطّاب (ḵuṭṭāb), plural of خاطِب (ḵāṭib).
From dialectal Arabic; compare Tunisian Arabic حشلاف (ḥušlāf, “hay, dried-out grass or plant”). Further origin uncertain, though Berber origin has been suggested.
Inherited from Arabic حُوَّارَى (ḥuwwārā). Compare regional Tunisian Arabic حوارات (ḥwārāt).

From Arabic زُجاج (zujāj, “glass”), a word with several variants (in Arabic and the Semitic languages at large). The Maltese form presupposes *خُجاج (*ḵujāj). Compare the even more distorted dialectal Arabic form قُزاز (quzāz); furthermore Hebrew זכוכית (zəḵūḵīṯ) alongside זגוגית (zəḡūḡīṯ). Doublet
From Arabic حُصَاص (ḥuṣāṣ, “mange, scab”), from حَصَّ (ḥaṣṣa, “to become hairless”), with voicing of ص (ṣ) as in several other Maltese words.

parole.significato: a person of doubtful sexual morals
parole.testo: Inherited from a Maghrebi Arabic word for “posterior”. Compare Tunisian Arabic زعكة (zaʕka, “woman’s buttocks”). Probably at first used for a homosexual man (treated as the main sense by Vassalli) and then generalised.
From Arabic *زَغْزُوغ (*zaḡzūḡ), variant of زَعْزُوع (zaʕzūʕ, “thin, meagre, lanky”) from زعزع (“to shake”); compare زُغْزُغ (zuḡzuḡ, “short, small”).

parole.significato: several flowers, blossoms (reproductive structures on some plants)
to go away or get out of the way

parole.testo: From Arabic زَمَّ (zamma, “to bind, tie up”).

From Arabic زِقّ (ziqq, “skin bag for liquids, waterskin”), from Classical Syriac ܙܩܐ (zeqqā, “idem”), which might be a variant of ܣܩܐ (saqqā, “sack, bag”). The last is cognate with Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sack, bag, sackcloth”), whence also English sack and Maltese saqqu (“mattress”).

From regional Arabic زَرْبُون (zarbūn), also زَرْبُول (zarbūl, “slipper, sandal, boot, stiletto”, etc., depending on dialect), from Ancient Greek σέρβουλα (sérboula, “shoe, buskin”), from Latin servulus, servula (“slave”) through some sort of figurative use. There is no relation with phonetically si
From Arabic زَرْجُون (zarjūn). See there for more.

From Arabic زَرْزَرَ (zarzara), related with زَرْزُور (zarzūr, “starling”, some of whose cries resemble insects’ chirring or buzzing). Compare also Moroccan Arabic سرسر (sarsar). Ultimately onomatopoeic.
Inherited from Arabic زَوَّلَ (zawwala). Compare Moroccan Arabic زول (zawwal).

parole.significato: to colour, paint, varnish, dye (apply colour to, in any context)
parole.testo: From Arabic صَبَغَ (ṣabaḡa), with generalisation of the regular assimilation [sb] → [zb].
From Arabic زَنْبُوج (zanbūj), زَبُّوج (zabbūj), eventually probably from Berber. Compare Moroccan Arabic زبوج (zabbūj, “(wild) olive tree”), Tunisian Arabic زبوز (zabbūz, “(wild) olive tree”).

parole.significato: to vilify, to abuse, to defame, to blaspheme
parole.testo: Inherited from a dialectal Arabic زَبْلَحَ (zablaḥa). The sense varies somewhat, but appears to be related to idle or dishonest talk. Possibly related with żżagħbel and Arabic خُزَعْبَلة (ḵuzaʕbala, “made-up and ridiculous story, palaver”). Or perhaps an extended form of the root ز ب ل (z b l); comp

parole.significato: to cover in tar or pitch
to neigh (make the sound of a horse)
parole.testo: From Arabic صَهَلَ (ṣahala, “to neigh”). Variation between -l- and -r- occurs frequently in Maltese. For the sporadic development of Arabic ص (ṣ) → Maltese ż compare żnuber.

From Arabic بُزَيْزة (buzayza), diminutive of بِزّ (bizz). For the loss of initial b- compare Algerian Arabic زيزة (zīza, “breast”, also “vulva” and “little boy’s penis”). Hence etymologically related to bażiż.

parole.significato: to fornicate; to commit adultery or any sexual sin
a narrow path, especially a minor country lane

parole.testo: Probably an extended form of żelaq, from Arabic زَلَقَ (zalaqa).

parole.significato: to variegate, to paint or decorate in various colours
to wed; to marry (officially join two people in marriage)

parole.testo: From Arabic زَوْج (zawj, “pair”), from Ancient Greek ζεῦγος (zeûgos, “yoke”). Compare Tunisian Arabic زُوز (zūz) and Moroccan Arabic جوج (jūj).
Inherited from Arabic زِيَادَة (ziyāda). Cognate with Tunisian Arabic زِادَة (zēdə)
From Arabic زَغَّلَ (zaḡḡala), أَزْغَلَ (ʔazḡala, “to feed one’s young”).
From Arabic زَامِل (zāmil, “horse or wild ass”), related to زَامِلَة (zāmila, “(she-)camel used to carry something”).

parole.significato: lewd, promiscuous, adulterous; (especially religion) given to or constituting sexual sin
fornication, adultery, or any sexual sin
parole.testo: From Arabic زِنَى (zinā). Predominantly feminised because of the final -a, though the original masculine is still found.

parole.significato: pitcher (a wide-mouthed, deep vessel for holding liquids)

parole.testo: From Arabic زِنَاد (zinād), originally plural of زَنْد (zand), but also used interchangeably.
From Arabic صَنَوْبَر (ṣanawbar, “pine”) with sporadic voicing of the onset.
Inherited from Arabic صِغَر (ṣiḡar). Compare Moroccan Arabic صغر (ṣḡur).
From Arabic زُكْرَة (zukra, “small hose”), thus probably originally referring to the umbilical cord or navel-string.
Inherited from Arabic زُرَافَة (zurāfa). Doublet of ġiraff.
From Arabic أَزْرَار (ʔazrār), plural of زِرّ (zirr). Compare Moroccan Arabic مزرار (muzrār, “gravel”).

From a Maghrebi Arabic form akin to Moroccan Arabic جران (jrān), from a Berber language; compare Northern Saharan Berber ajru and Tashelhit agru. Possibly from an alteration of Latin rāna with initial g- imitating the croaking sound of a frog, as in Catalan granota and French grenouille.

parole.significato: to frolic, disport oneself, pass time with idle amusement
parole.testo: The sense “to mock, make fun of” is attested in Panzavecchia's Bible translation (earlier 19th c.), hence the original meaning may have been “to joke, talk idly”. Perhaps related with Arabic خُزَعْبِل (ḵuzaʕbil, “made-up and ridiculous story, palaver”). Compare also żeblaħ.

Probably inherited from dialectal Arabic; compare especially Tunisian Arabic فرططو/فرفطو (farṭaṭṭu/farfaṭṭu), Moroccan Arabic فرططو (farṭuṭṭu, “butterfly”), but also Moroccan Arabic فرطوط (farṭūṭ, “moth”) etc. Eventually from Berber; compare Kabyle aferṭeṭṭu. The second -f- might be due to influence

Eventually from Latin fascia. Regarding the preserved velar/uvular, the form cannot have passed through Sicilian fascia, whence indeed Maltese faxxa.
